description: Removes a gbuild feature's entire local footprint — every worktree it opened (the feature worktree and each node's), its feature and node branches, the Relate store, and the inbox — after checking the graph's state and where its work landed, with one confirmation listing everything that dies. Local only — never the remote, never the user's own checkout. Use when the feature's PR is merged and the graph is no longer needed, or the feature is abandoned for good.
---

Remove the local footprint of the feature `$ARGUMENTS` (the slug): every worktree gbuild opened for it,
its branches, and its store — everything under `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<slug>/` dies with the feature.
`pr` published the branch; this reclaims what it left behind on this machine.

**CRITICAL: local only, destructive, confirmed.** This skill never touches the remote — never pushes,
never deletes a remote branch, never closes a PR — and never removes or re-branches the user's own
checkout or another feature's worktrees. It deletes exactly one feature's local footprint, and only
after the step-3 confirmation.

## Step 0: Resolve the slug — never infer it

`$ARGUMENTS` must name the feature explicitly: the first token that isn't a flag. Cleanup deletes the
feature's whole local footprint, so it never guesses a slug the way `review` and `pr` do. Empty →
list what exists — one line per directory under `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/` — and stop, asking the user
to re-invoke with a slug. Nothing exists there → say so and stop: there is nothing to clean up.

## Step 1: Establish VCS facts

Default to `git`. Resolve, absolute: `GC` = `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, `WT` = `GC/gbuild/<slug>`,
`DB` = `WT/db`, `INBOX` = `WT/inbox`. Locate the feature branch and worktree read-only — unlike
`/gbuild:run`'s step 0 this never attaches a worktree (creating one just to delete it is noise):

1. `WT/tree` is a registered worktree (`git worktree list --porcelain`) → `FT` = it, `BRANCH` =
   `git -C FT branch --show-current`.
2. Else a registered worktree whose branch is `<slug>` or ends `/<slug>` → `FT` = that worktree's path
   (a legacy feature). When gbuild did not open it — it is the user's own checkout, or a worktree on
   neither `WT` nor the harness placement this feature's worktrees follow — nothing is removed there,
   and a branch checked out there cannot be deleted; say so in the report.
3. Else a branch named `<slug>` or ending `/<slug>` exists (`git branch --list`) → `BRANCH` = it; no
   `FT` (it is checked out nowhere).
4. Else no feature branch: with `WT` present, only the store, inbox and leftovers remain — steps 2–4
   still clean them; without `WT` there is nothing left — say so and stop.

`NODE_WTS` = every registered worktree on a `gbuild/<slug>/*` branch — wherever it lives, including a
harness worktree placement (`/gbuild:run`'s step 0) — and `FT` is never on such a branch.
`NODE_BRANCHES` = `git branch --list 'gbuild/<slug>/*'`. Both are interrupted-run leftovers by
definition — `run` removes each the moment its node is accepted or terminally fails — so they are
unaccepted work and always removed with force, no questions asked.

## Step 2: Read the store

`DB` present → `relate --version` first (missing or older than 1.0.1 → stop: gbuild needs it, and
this skill will not delete a store it could not read). Store rules as ever: one `relate` command at
a time, `--read-only --mode jsonl` (one JSON object per row, zero rows print nothing — no output =
no rows; never `--timings`, whose telemetry line is not a row), on `storage locked` wait and retry up to 3 times;
the full manual is `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/cypher.md`.

```
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/progress.cypher
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/attention.cypher
```

No `DB` → the store is already gone (or was never charted); say so — the git work below is the whole
job. A gbuild ≤ 0.7.1 store may instead sit git-tracked at `FT/.gbuild/` — when `FT` survives cleanup
(a legacy feature in the user's checkout), list that directory in the inventory and leave removing it
to the user (`git rm -r --cached .gbuild`, per `reference/cypher.md`); when `FT` is removed, it dies
with the worktree.

## Step 3: Assemble the inventory, confirm once

Everything below dies in one confirmation, so gather it all first:

- **Graph state.** Every `progress` row with a non-empty `open` — the feature is not finished.
  `attention`: `in_progress` means a run may be active or interrupted — confirm no `/gbuild:run` is in
  flight before deleting anything; `failed` and `blocked-by-failed` name the stuck work being thrown
  away.
- **Uncommitted changes in `FT`** (`git -C FT status --porcelain`): they die with the worktree — list
  the files.
- **Where the work landed**, when `BRANCH` exists:
  - merged into its upstream — `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref BRANCH@{upstream}` resolves and
    `git merge-base --is-ancestor BRANCH <upstream>` is true → **landed**. (A squash-merged PR leaves
    the branch unmerged by ancestry, so also:)
  - else a merged PR — `gh pr list --head BRANCH --state merged` returns one, when `gh` is installed
    and authenticated → **landed**.
  - else another local branch contains it — `git branch --contains BRANCH` lists one besides
    `BRANCH` itself (which is always listed) → **landed** (merged locally, no remote involved).
  - else **not landed**. Show what a deletion would lose:
    `git log --oneline BRANCH --not --exclude=BRANCH --branches --remotes --tags | head -20` — the
    commits reachable from `BRANCH` and from no other ref. Empty list → every commit lives on
    somewhere (a pushed remote ref, another branch), so `-D` loses nothing local-only; non-empty →
    these commits exist only on this machine, and deleting the branch takes `git branch -D` and
    loses them.

Present the complete inventory — the feature and `BRANCH`; `NODE_WTS` and `NODE_BRANCHES` (always
deleted); `FT` (removed when gbuild opened it — under `WT`, or placed by the harness convention its
feature's worktrees follow — and left alone otherwise); the uncommitted files, if any; `DB`,
`INBOX` and everything else under `WT`, the feature's whole memory; the graph state; landed or not —
and ask once. Anything unfinished, uncommitted, unlanded, or possibly mid-run is called out
explicitly; the user confirms all of it or nothing. No → stop; nothing is deleted.

## Step 4: Delete

In this order — a worktree under `WT` cannot be `rm -rf`'d while registered, and a branch cannot be
deleted while checked out:

1. Node leftovers: `git worktree remove --force` each `NODE_WTS` entry, then `git branch -D` each
   `NODE_BRANCHES` entry.
2. `FT`, when gbuild opened it — under `WT`, or placed by the harness convention this feature's
   worktrees follow: `git worktree remove --force FT`.
3. `BRANCH`, when it exists: `git branch -d BRANCH` first — success is git's own proof that HEAD or the
   upstream contains the work. Refusal is not a verdict (git cannot see a squash-merged PR or a local
   merge), so fall back to the step-3 loss list: empty → `git branch -D BRANCH`, nothing local-only
   dies; non-empty → `git branch -D BRANCH` only on the user's confirmation of those commits. A
   refusal naming a worktree — the branch is checked out in a legacy `FT` — → leave it and report.
4. What is left of `WT`: `rm -rf WT` — the store, the inbox, anything else — then
   `rmdir GC/gbuild 2>/dev/null || true` (only succeeds when no other feature's directory remains),
   and `git worktree prune` to drop stale registrations an interrupted removal may have left.

## Step 5: Report

What was removed — worktrees, branches, the store — and what was kept, with its reason: the remote
branch (never touched), a legacy `BRANCH` still checked out in the user's own checkout, an unlanded
branch the user chose to keep (give its one-liner: `git branch -D <branch>`, should they change their
mind). A cleanup is the end of a feature — no `next:` line follows it.

Ends only when the human calls the design good; re-invoking with the slug resumes from the committed artifacts. ---

Design the feature described by `$ARGUMENTS` — with the human, before `/gbuild:plan` charts it.

`plan` decomposes a feature that already makes sense: a one-line destination, a scope with edges,
constraints it can verify against. When the work isn't there yet — the destination still has
options, the moving parts aren't named, the trade-offs are unmade — this skill shapes it into
committed artifacts first. It writes the design onto the feature branch and stops: no graph, no
store, no implementation. The committed artifacts are the design's whole state, so re-invoking
`/gbuild:design <slug>` resumes exactly where the commits left off. After it, `/gbuild:plan <slug>`
has a design to decompose instead of a guess.

## Mode

| arguments                                                 | mode                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| a description, link, or file path                         | **Design** — new feature                            |
| a slug with a feature worktree or branch, and no store    | **Resume** — continue the committed artifacts      |
| a slug whose store already exists                         | **Redirect** — `/gbuild:plan <slug> --add "<req>"`  |

`$ARGUMENTS` is slug-shaped only if it is one kebab-case token. Then, in order: a store at
`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<slug>/db` (its `graph.json` present) means `plan` already charted the
feature — don't design a charted feature; say so and point at `/gbuild:plan <slug> --add
"<requirement>"`, which is how a charted feature takes new work. A feature worktree or a branch
named `<slug>` or ending `/<slug>`, with no store, means a design started here and wasn't charted —
resume it. Anything else is a description — design it.

## Design

### 1. Slug, branch, and feature worktree

Derive the feature slug from `$ARGUMENTS`: kebab-case, ≤4 words, names the outcome not the mechanism
(`oauth-device-flow`, not `add-some-auth-stuff`). It names the artifact home below and the
`gbuild/<slug>/` directory `plan` later creates — immutable once the design is committed.

If the derived slug's store already exists (`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<slug>/db`), stop: the feature
is charted, and new work goes to `/gbuild:plan <slug> --add`. Resolve `FT` (the feature worktree)
exactly as `/gbuild:plan`'s Chart step 1 describes (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/plan/SKILL.md`) —
reuse the registered worktree, attach a branch checked out nowhere, or create branch and worktree
forked from the current HEAD. Report the branch and `FT`; everything below happens in `FT`. If
`docs/design/<slug>/` on that branch already has committed artifacts, this is a resume that arrived
as a description — read them (Resume below) instead of writing over them.

### 2. Analyse the codebase

Read the project manifest(s), directory structure, `README.md`, and the code the feature touches.
Resolve file paths or URLs in `$ARGUMENTS`; if a reference fails to load, say so and ask. For
related in-flight work — best-effort, never required: when `relate` is on PATH, read the
`Feature` of every existing store (`feature.cypher` with `--read-only` against each
`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/*/db`, one at a time); when it isn't, skip — this skill needs neither
`relate` nor a store, and never installs or creates either.

### 3. Fix the artifact home

The design artifacts live at `docs/design/<slug>/` on the feature branch; the entry doc is
`design.md`, and everything else hangs off it. Before writing anything, look at how the repo already
documents work — `docs/` layout, ADR or decision-record folders, README patterns — and follow an
existing convention when one is present: supporting docs take the repo's naming and format; only
the home and the entry doc are fixed here.

### 4. The design loop

The design is written by discussing it, one settled piece at a time. The loop runs until the human
calls the design good — never less, and never on your own judgement of when it's good enough.

1. **Open with what the analysis found.** A few lines: the pieces that exist, the gap, the
   constraints — grounding, not a report. End with the first batch of questions.
2. **Ask in batches.** Put the round's open questions to the human in one message — cap at ~5. The
   destination comes first, and it must end up one line, the thing that is true once this is done;
   everything past it is scope to defend or cut. Then what the destination needs decided: scope
   edges, naming, the trade-offs with real alternatives, the risks worth stating. Never one question
   at a time, and never 20 questions — a round with more than ~5 open questions hasn't converged:
   settle what the last answers gave you, and batch the rest into the next round.
3. **Settle as they solidify.** Fold each round's answers into the artifacts the moment they're
   agreed, and commit — message `docs(design/<slug>): <what settled>` — so an interruption costs
   nothing that had settled. `design.md` carries the state: the destination (one line), the scope
   and out-of-scope, what the analysis found, each decision with its rationale and the alternatives
   it ruled out, and the open questions still in play. Supporting docs — whatever this design
   needs: diagrams, data shapes, interface sketches — follow the repo's convention (step 3).
4. **An unknown that needs code is an open question, not a prototype.** Design writes no
   implementation — no scaffolding, no probes, no spike branches. A question the analysis can't
   answer by reading goes into `design.md`'s open questions for `/gbuild:plan` to chart as a
   `research` node.

### 5. Report and hand over

Only after the human has called the design good: ask nothing more, write and commit the last of it,
then report the artifacts (every file under `docs/design/<slug>/`), the branch, and `FT`. The feature
worktree stays — `plan` reuses it. Then both exits, the human's to pick:

- **Continue into gbuild** — `next: /gbuild:plan <slug>`.
- **A design review on a PR** — ask the agent to open it directly with `gh` from `FT` (push the
  branch, `gh pr create`): `/gbuild:pr` can't, it needs a graph store, and a design isn't charted.

## Resume

Re-invoking `/gbuild:design <slug>` continues a design the feature worktree or branch already holds —
the mode table routed you here:

0. Resolve `FT` exactly as step 1 describes — reuse the registered worktree, attach the branch if
   it's checked out nowhere. Never into the user's main checkout unless that's where the feature
   branch already lives (a legacy feature).
1. Read the committed artifacts at `docs/design/<slug>/` in `FT`. `design.md` says what's decided
   and what's open; the commit log says what settled when. Anything the loop left uncommitted never
   settled — start that piece over.
2. Continue the loop (step 4) from the open questions. A settled decision reopens only on new
   information, said out loud — not on a fresh context's second thoughts.

## Rules

- **Design, don't build.** Nothing lands on the branch but the artifacts under
  `docs/design/<slug>/` — no implementation, no scaffolding, no probes. Unknowns that need code
  become open questions for `plan` to chart as `research` nodes.
- **The human closes the design.** The loop ends on the human calling it good, never on your own
  judgement; the closing report follows that word and nothing before it.
- **Commit as work solidifies.** Everything agreed is written and committed in the round it was
  agreed in — the branch is the state, there is no store, and an interrupted design must resume
  having lost nothing that had settled.
- **No relate, no store.** This skill runs without either and never installs or creates
  either: a store's existence only routes the mode, and sibling stores are read best-effort
  (step 2), only when `relate` is already on PATH.
- **The user's checkout never changes branch.** Every edit, commit, and check happens in `FT`; the
  main tree is never touched.

Creates the feature branch in its own git worktree, never touching the main checkout. Use when starting new gbuild work, before /gbuild:run.

Plan the work described in `$ARGUMENTS` as a graph.

## The loop

The intended workflow: `/gbuild:design <slug>` when the work needs shaping, ordinary conversation
when it doesn't, then chart it here. After this skill: `/gbuild:run <slug>` once — it starts each
node as its dependencies complete, until the graph completes. Then `/gbuild:review <slug>`; if it
finds issues, reopen with `/gbuild:plan <slug> --add "<fix>"` and `/gbuild:run` again; if clean,
`/gbuild:pr <slug>`.

Read `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/graph-format.md` (the normative graph model) and
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/cypher.md` (how to talk to the store) before doing anything, and run
its version check. `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/shapes.md`,
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/failure-policies.md`, and `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/cost-model.md`
inform the choices below. `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/checklist.md` is the self-check at the end.

## Mode

| arguments                                    | mode                    |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| a description, link, or file path             | **Chart** — new feature |
| an existing feature slug with `--add "<req>"` | **Reopen**              |

A bare slug with no store is a description, not a slug — chart it. A slug's store lives beside its
feature worktree at `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<slug>/db`, machine-local and never committed (a gbuild ≤ 0.7.1
store needs the move in `reference/cypher.md`).

## Chart

### 1. Slug, branch, and feature worktree

Derive the feature slug from `$ARGUMENTS`: kebab-case, ≤4 words, names the outcome not the mechanism
(`oauth-device-flow`, not `add-some-auth-stuff`). It's the `gbuild/<slug>/` directory name and the
`Feature` node's `feature` property — immutable once charted.

gbuild never changes the branch of the user's checkout: the feature branch lives in its own **feature
worktree**, so several features can be charted and run in parallel without racing each other's `HEAD`,
and uncommitted work in the main tree is irrelevant — there is no dirty-tree check. Resolve these paths,
all absolute: `GC` = `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` (resolve it to an absolute path), `WT` =
`GC/gbuild/<slug>` — the feature's worktree root, inside `.git/` so nothing under it is ever committed —
and `FT` = `WT/tree`, the feature worktree, the one place the feature branch is checked out. Then:

- `FT` is already a registered worktree (`git worktree list --porcelain`) → reuse it, say so.
- A branch named `<slug>` or ending `/<slug>` already exists → if it's checked out somewhere (a feature
  charted before the worktree layout usually has it in the main tree), that location is `FT`; otherwise
  attach it: `git worktree add FT <branch>`.
- Otherwise create branch and worktree in one step, forked from the current HEAD:

  ```
  git worktree add FT -b <prefix>/<slug> HEAD
  ```

  Take `<prefix>` from the repo's convention — project or user instructions first, else the dominant
  pattern in `git branch --list` — and fall back to `gbuild` when there is none.

**Worktree placement follows the harness when it has a convention.** The default above puts the
feature worktree at `WT/tree` (and `run` later puts each node worktree at `WT/<node-slug>`) — inside
`.git/`, invisible to `git status`, never committed. But when the harness this skill runs in has its
own worktree convention — its tooling or instructions say where worktrees live and how they're named,
or the repo's registered worktrees (`git worktree list --porcelain`) already show one clear pattern —
create `FT` there instead, named its way, with its creation tooling where it offers one; `run`
follows the same rule for node worktrees. gbuild's own conventions hold regardless: the
`<prefix>/<slug>` branch name, `DB` and `INBOX` staying under `WT`, and worktrees being resolved by
their branch, never by path.

Report the branch and `FT`. Everything below happens in `FT`; `DB` below is `WT/db`.

### 2. Analyse the codebase

Read the project manifest(s), directory structure, `README.md`, and — for related in-flight work — the
`Feature` of every existing store (`feature.cypher` with `--read-only` against each `GC/gbuild/*/db`,
one at a time). Resolve
file paths or URLs in `$ARGUMENTS`; if a reference fails to load, say so and ask. When `FT` holds the
feature's design artifacts — committed by `/gbuild:design` at `docs/design/<slug>/`, entry doc
`design.md`, everything else hanging off it — read all of them first: they are the design context the
graph is charted from; its settled decisions are facts to decompose, not questions to reopen. When
no design is at `docs/design/<slug>/` in `FT`, check `docs/design/*` in `FT` before charting
fresh: a re-described feature — the same work, described again under a different slug — still
finds its committed design that way, and it is read exactly as above.

### 3. Validate and explore

Triage `$ARGUMENTS` against what step 2 found. The point is to catch plans that are wrong *before*
they're charted — not to interrogate every input. If the description is sharp and the scope is
unambiguous, this step is a quick confirmation and you move on.

**Classify the input into one of:**

- **Clear** — names a concrete outcome, scope is unambiguous, no assumption risky enough to
  invalidate the graph if wrong. This is the default when a competent spec lands. Skip to step 4.
  Don't manufacture questions for a plan that already makes sense.
- **Gappy** — missing constraints, ambiguous terms, or a destination that could mean two different
  things. Ask. Batch **all** clarifying questions in one message; cap at ~5. If you need more, the
  input is underspecified — say so and ask the user to rewrite it rather than play 20 questions.
  Fold the answers in, then proceed.
- **Risky** — the plan rests on an assumption that, if wrong, invalidates nodes or edges (a library
  can do X, a data source exists at a given shape, a perf budget holds). Don't just ask about it —
  **resolve** it. Find evidence in the codebase or docs, or chart a prototype (below). State the
  assumption, what's at risk, and how you resolved it. A resolved assumption is a fact the graph
  rests on; an unresolved one is a hole.

**Explore alternatives when the destination doesn't dictate the mechanism.** If two plausible
approaches reach the outcome, name each in one sentence, pick one, say why in one sentence. Skip
the survey when there's only one real way — don't perform thoroughness for its own sake.

**Prototypes are nodes, not side quests.** An unknown that needs code or a probe to resolve becomes
a `research`-typed GbuildNode in the first wave — `plan` charts it, `run` executes it. `plan` does
not run prototypes inline (the "Plan, don't do" rule below). The one exception: a check so cheap it
finishes in a single tool call (grep, read a file, check an installed version) — do that inline and
note the result. A prototype worth charting names the specific question it answers in its `OUTPUT`
field, and its `acceptance` is the answer to that question.

### 4. Name the destination

Ask, one question at a time, until `destination` fits in one line — the thing that's true once this is
done. Do not proceed until it's that sharp; everything past it goes in `out_of_scope`.

### 5. Decompose into nodes, not steps

List the real pieces of work. For each pair, apply the **cut test** (`graph-format.md`): does one
actually read the other's output? If no, they're independent — same wave, not a chain. This is the step
hone-ai v1 skipped, and the whole reason gbuild exists: state the true dependency structure, don't
default to the order you thought of things in.

**Chart the largest node one context can implement precisely.** Every node costs a dispatch, a
review, a worktree and a merge, so a graph of many small nodes is slower than the same work in fewer
solid ones — the agents `run` dispatches hold whole features these days; don't decompose for a weaker
agent than you're actually sending. Where one node would merely produce a value a single consumer
reads, and one context could do both halves precisely, make them one node — that edge is pure ceremony.
What stays separate is the real structure: work that genuinely runs in parallel, genuinely fails
independently, or genuinely needs its own context.

Classify each cluster's shape per `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/shapes.md` (chain / diamond / router /
controlled cycle). A controlled cycle needs its round cap and dedup rule decided now, not left to `run`
to invent.

For each GbuildNode decide (full model in `graph-format.md`):

- `slug` — kebab-case, immutable; what skills and the store key on. `title` — what the user reads.
- `type` — `research | decision | code | test | verify | chore`, plus the matching PascalCase label.
  `research`, `decision` and `verify` nodes get no worktree and edit no files — they deliver through
  their `OUTPUT` values only. Anything that must land in the repo (an ADR, a doc, a config file) belongs
  to a `code` node that reads those outputs through `FROM`.
- **`OUTPUT` fields** — every node declares at least one, each with a precise `shape`
  (`<integer>`, `<list of changed file paths>`, `<commit sha>`). Values will be scalars or lists of
  scalars; for anything nested, the shape says it is a JSON-encoded string.
- **`INPUT` fields** — one per value the node reads. If it comes from another node, wire it
  `FROM` that node's `OUTPUT` field and add the `DEPENDS_ON`. If it comes from the codebase or the
  environment, leave it without `FROM` and say where in its `shape`. The cut test is now concrete:
  a `DEPENDS_ON` exists exactly when the node reads one of the other's outputs.
- `acceptance` — **mandatory, non-empty, concrete, and narrow.** No vague adjectives. A criterion a
  fresh context with no other information couldn't check is not concrete enough — rewrite it until it
  names a file, a shape, a value, or a command's result. Then make it the narrowest check that proves
  it — a specific test file or a scoped command, not a repo-wide suite: the implementer runs what the
  criteria name and the reviewer re-runs it, so one broad criterion makes every gate heavy (the full
  suite runs once, in the end-of-feature audit). And keep the bar honest — a criterion that asks for
  more than the destination, the user's requirements, or the repo's architecture call for builds
  over-engineering into every node that satisfies it.
- `verify` — only when the node needs something *beyond* the standard `gbuild-reviewer` pass. Usually
  omitted.
- `failure_policy` — per `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/failure-policies.md`, don't default everything
  to `retry`. `model_tier` — `strong` only where judgement, not throughput, is the bottleneck.
  `review` — `mechanical` only where a named, scoped command or a shape check proves the whole bar
  (`reference/cost-model.md`); unset means `reviewer`, which is right for anything judgement must
  grade.
- `status: 'pending'` — every new node starts pending.

### 6. Write the global acceptance bar

The feature-level bar is one `Acceptance` node per bullet (`id` `a-1`, `a-2`, …), each linked
`(:Feature)-[:HAS_ACCEPTANCE]->(:Acceptance)`. Every bullet must end up covered by at least one node's
`SATISFIES` edge — the validator enforces it.

### 7. Self-check against the checklist

Walk every item in `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/checklist.md` against the graph you designed. Fix the
design, don't annotate around a failing item.

### 8. Create the store and write the graph

Create the store exactly as `reference/cypher.md` § Creating a store shows (`mkdir -p DB`, then
`schema.cypher` with `--snapshot-format json`).

Then write the whole graph as **one** Cypher script, piped through a quoted heredoc.
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/templates/example.cypher` is a complete worked example — follow its structure:
`.begin`, a single statement of `CREATE` clauses (so variables like `a1` or `a_value` stay in scope for
the edges), `.commit`.

```
relate query --database DB <<'CYPHER'
.begin
CREATE (f:Feature {feature: '<slug>', destination: '...', context: '...', out_of_scope: ['...']})
CREATE (a1:Acceptance {id: 'a-1', text: '...'})
CREATE (f)-[:HAS_ACCEPTANCE]->(a1)
CREATE (n:GbuildNode:Code {slug: '...', title: '...', type: 'code', acceptance: ['...'],
                           failure_policy: 'repair', model_tier: 'cheap', status: 'pending'})
CREATE (n)-[:OUTPUT]->(n_out:Field {name: '...', shape: '<...>'})
...
CREATE (m)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(n)
CREATE (m)-[:INPUT]->(:Field {name: '...', shape: '<...>'})-[:FROM]->(n_out)
CREATE (m)-[:SATISFIES]->(a1);
.commit
CYPHER
```

A constraint violation (`ConstraintValidationFailed`: a missing property, a wrong type, a duplicate
slug) fails the transaction and writes nothing — fix the script and run it again.

### 9. Validate

```
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/validate.cypher
```

No row records means valid. Every row is a violation (`check`, `detail`): fix it with Cypher — a `.begin` …
`.commit` script of `MATCH … SET/CREATE/DELETE` — and re-run until it returns no rows. Never
hand off a graph that fails validation, and never edit `graph.json` directly.

Then confirm run-readiness:

```
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/progress.cypher
```

One row per wave: each row's `open` slugs are the decomposition, and the `frontier` counts are what
`run` claims first. Nodes you expected to run together should share a wave.

### 10. Report and stop

There is nothing to commit — the store is machine-local, outside every checkout. Report the branch,
`FT`, the waves, and the frontier. Close with `next: /gbuild:run <slug>`.

## Reopen

`--add "<requirement>"`:

0. Resolve `FT` and `DB` exactly as Chart's step 1 describes (reuse the existing feature worktree;
   attach it if the branch is checked out nowhere). Never chart a reopen onto a different branch than
   the one the graph was charted on, and never into the user's main checkout unless that's where the
   feature branch already lives (a legacy feature).
1. Read the current graph narrowly: `progress.cypher` for its shape and what's done, and `node.cypher`
   only for the nodes the requirement touches.
2. Design the delta: a new `Acceptance` node (next `a-` id) linked from the `Feature`, and whatever new
   GbuildNodes it needs, with their `Field`s. A new node may depend on an already-completed one — wire
   its `INPUT` `FROM` that node's `OUTPUT` like any other; its value is already recorded. Re-run the
   checklist against the delta.
3. Write it as one script that `MATCH`es what it connects to and `CREATE`s the rest:

   ```
   relate query --database DB <<'CYPHER'
   .begin
   MATCH (f:Feature), (up:GbuildNode {slug: '<existing-slug>'})-[:OUTPUT]->(up_out:Field {name: '<field>'})
   CREATE (f)-[:HAS_ACCEPTANCE]->(a:Acceptance {id: 'a-3', text: '...'})
   CREATE (n:GbuildNode:Code {slug: '...', ..., status: 'pending'})
   CREATE (n)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(up)
   CREATE (n)-[:INPUT]->(:Field {name: '...', shape: '<...>'})-[:FROM]->(up_out)
   CREATE (n)-[:OUTPUT]->(:Field {name: '...', shape: '<...>'})
   CREATE (n)-[:SATISFIES]->(a);
   .commit
   CYPHER
   ```

4. **Re-run `validate.cypher`** until it returns no rows, then `progress.cypher`, and report the new
   frontier.

If the requirement needs no new nodes (an existing node's contract already covers it), say so and stop
— don't manufacture graph churn.

## Rules

- **Plan, don't do.** Nodes here get *defined*, not executed — even `research` nodes. They land in the
  first wave and `run` dispatches them.
- **The store is only touched through `relate`**, from this skill, one command at a time
  (`reference/cypher.md`).
- **Acceptance criteria are the bar, not a formality.** A node with vague acceptance is a node
  `gbuild-reviewer` can't actually check — that's a planning failure, not something to fix later.
- **Chart the natural path.** Shape the graph the way the evidence points: the user's description
  and wishes, the repo's existing architecture and conventions, and prior art in the wild — standards
  and common patterns for this kind of change. An abstraction, layer, or option those call for is the
  natural path, not gold-plating; one none of them calls for is — don't chart it. A leaner graph is a
  faster graph, but never leaner than the evidence.
- **Refer to nodes by title in anything the user reads.** Slugs are for the graph, not the conversation.

Publish a finished feature branch: push it to the right remote, open a well-formed pull request, then watch the PR's CI checks and drive a graph reopen automatically when a check goes red — looping until the checks are green or a round cap is hit.

## CRITICAL: main-context requirement

This skill MUST run in the **main conversation context**. It MUST NOT be invoked as a forked subagent (e.g. via the Agent/Task tool). The auto-fix step runs `/gbuild:run`, which dispatches one Agent per node — and forked agents cannot nest, so a nested fork will fail. If you are already running inside a forked agent, stop immediately and report that `/gbuild:pr` must be run from the top-level conversation.

## Step 0: Parse arguments

`$ARGUMENTS` is free-form text: an optional feature slug and an optional `--max-rounds N` flag.

- **slug**: the first token that isn't a flag. If absent, infer it — if exactly one feature worktree exists (`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/*/tree`), that's the slug; otherwise fall back to the most recently modified `graph.json` under `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/*/db`. If neither resolves, leave `<slug>` unresolved (the auto-fix step degrades gracefully — see Step 4).

When `<slug>` resolved, every graph read below goes through `relate`: run `relate --version` first (missing or older than 1.0.1 → stop; gbuild needs it), one command at a time, always `--read-only --mode jsonl` (one JSON object per row, zero rows print nothing — no output = no rows; never `--timings`, whose telemetry line is not a row; this skill only reads the store), and on `storage locked` wait and retry up to 3 times. Anything else: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/cypher.md`. `DB` below is `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<slug>/db`, beside the feature worktree (a gbuild ≤ 0.7.1 store needs the move in `reference/cypher.md`).
- **max_rounds**: the value of `--max-rounds N` (also accept `--max-rounds=N`). Default `3` when absent.

## Step 1: Preconditions

Verify the environment before touching the remote. Stop with a clear, actionable message if any check fails:

1. **Git repo.** This skill is git + GitHub specific. If the repo is not git, stop and explain that `/gbuild:pr` only supports git + GitHub (`gh`).
2. **GitHub CLI.** Confirm `gh` is installed and authenticated (`gh auth status`). If not, stop and tell the user to install/authenticate `gh`.
3. **Base branch.** Determine the upstream default branch: `gh repo view --json defaultBranchRef -q .defaultBranchRef.name`. Call it `<base>`.
4. **Feature worktree and branch.** Resolve `FT` (the feature worktree) and `<branch>` (the feature branch checked out there) exactly as `/gbuild:run`'s step 0 describes — the registered worktree (by default at `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<slug>/tree`, or wherever a harness worktree placement put it), a legacy feature whose branch is in the main tree, or attach a branch that is checked out nowhere. When `<slug>` is unresolved, use the main tree's current branch as `<branch>` and its root as `FT`. If `<branch>` equals `<base>`, stop — there is nothing to open a PR for.
5. **Clean tree.** Check for uncommitted changes in the feature worktree (`git -C FT status --porcelain`). `/gbuild:run` commits each node's work as it goes, so it should be clean. If there are uncommitted changes, warn the user and ask whether to proceed (they may want to commit first).
6. **Commits ahead of base.** Confirm the branch has commits the base lacks (`git log <base>..<branch> --oneline`). If empty, stop — nothing to push.
7. **Graph finished.** When `<slug>` resolved, run `relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/progress.cypher`. If any row's `open` is non-empty, warn that the graph isn't finished (name the open nodes) and ask whether to open the PR anyway. If any row has `failed` > 0, get their names from `attention.cypher` and name them — a PR built on an escalated node is usually premature.

## Step 2: Determine the remote & push

Choose the push remote from the project's actual remotes:

1. List remotes (`git remote -v`).
2. **Exactly one remote** → use it.
3. **Multiple remotes** → look for a push-target hint in `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` (e.g. an explicit statement that the project pushes to a fork). If a clear hint exists, use it. Otherwise, use `AskUserQuestion` to let the user pick which remote to push to (e.g. `origin` vs a fork remote).

Push the feature branch and set upstream: `git push -u <remote> <branch>` (branch names are refs — the
main tree's checkout is irrelevant).

## Step 3: Open the pull request

Build a **short, well-formed** description, then open the PR.

Gather context from:

- Commit subjects: `git log <base>..<branch> --oneline`.
- File overview: `git diff <base>...<branch> --stat`.
- When `<slug>` resolved: `relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/feature.cypher` — the `destination` and the acceptance bar (with the nodes covering each criterion).

Derive a concise, conventional-commit-style title from the feature/branch and the changes (e.g. `feat(auth): add OAuth login`).

Write the body to this template. Keep it tight — bullets, not essays. Classify what kind of change this is (new feature, fix, optimization, replacement, refactor, or other) and lead with that. Most changes are not user-facing — only include the **User-facing impact** and **Example usage** sections when something a user actually interacts with (API, CLI, config, UI, output) changed; omit them entirely otherwise. When you include them, the **Example usage** section goes right after **User-facing impact** and shows concrete sample input and the resulting output. Omit any section that has nothing:

```
## Summary
<1–2 sentences: what changed & why, and the kind of change — new feature / fix / optimization / replacement / refactor / other>

## Changes
- <bullet per notable change — what it does, not a play-by-play>

## User-facing impact
<Only when the change is user-facing: what users will now see or do differently (inputs and/or outputs). Drop this whole section for internal-only changes.>

## Example usage
<Only when the change is user-facing, immediately after User-facing impact: concrete before/after — sample input and the resulting output. Use fenced code blocks. Drop this whole section for internal-only changes.>

---
This description was auto generated
```

The trailing `This description was auto generated` line is **mandatory** — it always ends the body, after every other section, and is never dropped or reworded.

Create the PR: `gh pr create --base <base> --title "<title>" --body "<body>" --draft` — run it with `FT` as the working directory, so `gh` resolves the head from the feature branch (it handles fork `owner:branch` head refs automatically). Capture the PR URL and number (`<pr>`).

**Draft mode is not optional when the repo's agent contract (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) says so.** Before creating, check the repo's instructions for a draft-PR policy; if one exists (e.g. "open every PR as a draft; only a human marks it ready"), the PR MUST open as a draft and this skill NEVER converts it to ready — the green-checks report ends with the PR left in draft, and the human owns the ready flip. `--draft` is the safe default even without an explicit policy: a draft runs the fast gate only.

## Step 4: Monitor checks in the background → auto-fix loop

Watch the PR's CI checks and react when they fail. Run for at most `max_rounds` rounds:

1. **Launch the watch in the background.** Run `gh pr checks <pr> --watch --fail-fast` (from `FT`) via the Bash tool with `run_in_background: true`. It exits `0` when all checks pass and non-zero when a check fails; the harness re-invokes this skill when the command exits, so continue from the result.
2. **Checks green (exit 0):** report success and go to Step 5.
3. **Checks red (non-zero exit):**
   - Collect the failure detail: `gh pr checks <pr>` for the failed-check list, and `gh run view <run-id> --log-failed` for the failing logs.
   - **If `<slug>` is unresolved** (the branch wasn't produced by gbuild, so there's no graph to reopen): do not auto-fix. Print which checks failed with their logs and suggest the user fix manually, then go to Step 5 with an `unresolved` status.
   - **Otherwise, fix automatically** — via the graph, not by patching around it. gbuild has no separate fix skill; a red check is a new requirement:
     1. Read `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/plan/SKILL.md` and execute its **Reopen** path inline: `--add "<requirement>"` where the requirement is the failing check stated as a concrete outcome (e.g. `CI check "lint" passes — <the actual error>`). Re-read that file and follow it verbatim rather than paraphrasing it here, so this phase auto-syncs when `plan` changes. One requirement per distinct failing check.
     2. Run it unattended. `plan`'s Reopen asks nothing, but if executing it would prompt the user (an ambiguous decomposition), resolve it yourself from the failing logs and note the choice in the final report — `/gbuild:pr` runs without a human present.
     3. If Reopen concludes the requirement needs no new nodes, stop the loop and go to Step 5 with an `unresolved` status — the failure isn't something the graph can act on, so surface the logs to the user.
     4. Read `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/run/SKILL.md` and execute it inline against `<slug>` to run the newly-unblocked frontier. Suppress its trailing `next: /gbuild:status…` line — this skill owns the transition.
   - After the run completes, push the new commits (`git -C FT push`) and **re-launch the watch** (next round).

4. **Round cap reached while still red:** stop, print the still-failing checks and their logs, and tell the user to inspect manually. Go to Step 5 with an `unresolved` status.

## Step 5: Final output

Report the outcome:

```
PR: <url>  (checks: green | fixed after <rounds> round(s) | unresolved after <max_rounds> round(s))
next: /gbuild:status <slug>
```

graph is no longer needed, `/gbuild:cleanup <slug>` reclaims the feature's whole local footprint: every
worktree it opened, its branches, and the store — the whole `WT`, `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<slug>`,
dies with the feature.

This is not a second pass at what `gbuild-reviewer` already did. That agent grades one node against one
contract; this one grades what the whole accumulated diff did to the codebase — the duplication and
missed abstractions that only exist *between* nodes, which no per-node review can see.

## Arguments

`$ARGUMENTS` is optional. If present, treat it as the feature slug. If absent, infer it — if exactly one
feature worktree exists (`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/*/tree`), that's the slug; otherwise fall back to the
most recently modified `graph.json` under `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/*/db`. Do NOT write
any file — this skill outputs to chat exclusively.

Resolve `FT`, the feature worktree, exactly as `/gbuild:run`'s step 0 describes (reuse the registered
worktree, attach if the feature branch is checked out nowhere). `DB` below is
`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<slug>/db`, beside the worktree (a gbuild ≤ 0.7.1 store needs the move in
`reference/cypher.md`).

Store rules: run `relate --version` first (missing or older than 1.0.1 → stop; gbuild needs it).
One `relate` command at a time, always `--read-only --mode jsonl` (one JSON object per row, zero
rows print nothing — no output = no rows; never `--timings`, whose telemetry line is not a row;

Check the graph is finished — one row per wave, cheap:

```
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/progress.cypher
```

If any row's `open` is non-empty, say the graph isn't finished (name the open nodes) and ask whether to
audit anyway — auditing a half-built branch produces findings that the remaining nodes were going to

## Run the audit

Fetch the feature context:

```
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/feature.cypher
```

Launch the `gbuild-auditor` subagent (agents/gbuild-auditor.md — this plugin's own copy, gbuild does not
depend on hone-ai being installed). Pass it:

- The resolved slug and the `feature.cypher` result verbatim (destination and the acceptance bar with
  the nodes covering each criterion) — the auditor never opens the store itself, and reads the code from
  the branch diff.
- The feature worktree path `FT` and the feature branch name — it audits the branch's code from `FT`:
  every read, every check, and every git command runs there, never in the main tree.

The sub-agent runs the full audit in its own fresh context and returns the audit as its final message.
That message is a tool result — it is NOT shown to the user. So once it returns:

**Relay the sub-agent's entire output to chat verbatim, preserving its closing line exactly.** Do not
summarize, reorder, or rewrite it. The closing line is a contract:

- `Run /gbuild:plan <slug> --add "the above blocking issues"` — `plan`'s Reopen path resolves

Run the graph for the feature `$ARGUMENTS` (the slug; step 0 resolves `DB`, the store — the feature
branch lives in its own worktree, so this skill never changes the branch of the user's checkout).

**CRITICAL: this skill must run in the main context, not inside a forked agent.** It dispatches its own
subagents per node; a subagent cannot itself fan out further subagents reliably. It is also the store's
**only writer**: agents read their brief from the store themselves and leave their result in the inbox;
this skill passes them slugs and paths, reads their one-line replies, and records.

## Store rules

- `relate --version` first. If it's missing or older than 1.0.1, stop: gbuild needs it
  (`curl -sSfL https://relatedb.ai/install.sh | bash`, or `relate upgrade`).
- You are the only writer: `dispatch`, `set-status` and `record` run only here, one `relate` command
  at a time against `DB` — never parallel tool calls on it. Subagents may run `relate` only with
  `--read-only` (a read opens beside the writer); their agent files say what they read.
- Always `--mode jsonl`, never `--timings`: one JSON object per row and nothing else — N rows print
  exactly N lines, zero rows print nothing, so no output = no rows (`--timings` would append a
  per-statement telemetry line that is not a row). Every `--param` value is JSON,
  single-quoted for the shell (`--param 'slugs=["a","b"]'`); write a `'` inside it as `\u0027`.
- Pure reads (validate, attention, progress below) open the store `--read-only`; the writes
  (dispatch, set-status, record) stay writable — the CLI checkpoints a writable store on exit itself.
- `storage locked` (exit 5) → another writer holds the store: wait a few seconds, retry up to 3 times,
  then stop. Exit code 1 = failure; read stderr. Anything beyond the scripts below:
  `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/cypher.md`.
- Hold only what routes: dispatch rows, one reply line per agent, record rows. Never open a result file,
  a review file or a diff, and never type acceptance text or output values — the store and the inbox
  carry them.

## Step 0: Establish VCS facts, then check and recover

Default to `git`. Resolve these facts first, absolute paths, and reuse them throughout:

- `GC` = `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, resolved to an absolute path; `WT` = `GC/gbuild/$ARGUMENTS`
  (the feature's directory — the store, the inbox and, by default, its worktrees; inside `.git/`, so
  none of it appears in `git status` or gets committed).
- **Worktree placement.** Default: the feature worktree is `WT/tree` and each node worktree
  `WT/<slug>`. But when the harness has its own worktree convention — its tooling or instructions say
  where worktrees live and how they're named, or the repo's registered worktrees
  (`git worktree list --porcelain`) show one clear pattern — follow it instead for every worktree this
  skill creates: place them where it puts worktrees, name them the way it names them, use its
  creation tooling where it offers one. gbuild's own conventions hold regardless: the branch names,
  `DB` and `INBOX` staying under `WT`, and resolving worktrees by their branch, never by path.
- `FT` = the feature worktree and `BRANCH` = the feature branch — the one place `BRANCH` is checked
  out, and where every merge below lands:
  1. `WT/tree` is a registered worktree (`git worktree list --porcelain`) → `FT` = it, `BRANCH` =
     `git -C FT branch --show-current`.
  2. Else a worktree whose branch is `$ARGUMENTS` or ends `/$ARGUMENTS` → `FT` = that worktree's path
     (a feature charted before the worktree layout usually has its branch in the main tree; a harness
     placement may have put it elsewhere).
  3. Else such a branch exists but is checked out nowhere → attach it where the placement rule puts
     the feature worktree (default `git worktree add WT/tree <branch>`), `FT` = that path.
  4. Else → stop: there is no feature branch for `$ARGUMENTS` — chart it with `/gbuild:plan` first.
- `DB` = `WT/db` — the feature's store, beside the worktree: machine-local, never committed (a gbuild ≤ 0.7.1
  store needs the move in `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/cypher.md`).
- `INBOX` = `WT/inbox` — beside `DB`, outside every worktree: each implementer writes `<slug>.json`
  there and each reviewer `<slug>.review.json` when it fails (a pass writes none); only
  `record.cypher` reads them, on your behalf.

Then check and recover:

```
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/validate.cypher
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/attention.cypher
```

- `validate` returning any row → stop and report the rows; do not run a graph `plan` didn't finish
  correctly.
- `attention` rows with reason `in_progress` are left over from an interrupted run (this skill is the
  only writer and records every node before finishing). Check each one's worktree branch for commits
  its agent already made (`git log BRANCH..gbuild/<feature>/<slug>` — empty
  means it never got that far) and leave the worktree in place: the re-dispatch reuses it. Then reset
  them all in one call so they re-dispatch, and mention it in the report:

  ```
  relate query --database DB --mode jsonl --param 'slugs=["<slug>", ...]' --param 'status="pending"' \
    < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/set-status.cypher
  ```

- Sweep for worktree leaks from an interruption that struck mid-cleanup: any registered worktree
  (`git worktree list --porcelain`) on a branch `gbuild/$ARGUMENTS/<slug>` — wherever it lives — whose
  slug is *not* among the slugs just reset does not belong to live work — remove it
  (`git worktree remove --force`) and delete its branch (`git branch -D`). An unmerged
  branch is unaccepted work, which must never land — that is what the isolation is for. `FT` is never
  on such a branch, so the sweep can never touch it.
- Create the inbox empty. This discards the files of the nodes just reset — an interrupted attempt is
  never recorded; they re-dispatch from scratch on top of their surviving worktrees:

  ```
  mkdir -p WT/inbox
  find WT/inbox -type f -delete
  ```

## Step 1: Pick a backend

**Workflow tool**, whenever this session has it — no opt-in needed; gbuild's run is exactly the
multi-agent fan-out that tool exists for. One `pipeline()` per claimed node: its implement `agent()`,
then — for a `reviewer`-tier node — its `gbuild-reviewer` `agent()`, prompted exactly as in step 2.2
and read as in step 2.3. A `mechanical` node's pipeline is its implementer alone: land and record it
from the main context through step 2.3's mechanical gate. A review starts the moment its implementer
finishes and no node waits on another, so this backend does not batch reviews — batching (step 2.3)
exists to cut spin-ups where the handoff can't be pipelined. Nodes use the worktrees step 2.2
creates (no `isolation` option: the prompt names the worktree). Controlled-cycle clusters become a
bounded `while` loop per `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/shapes.md`'s round cap. Route
`model_tier: strong` nodes via `opts.model` where the harness supports an override. The script never
touches the store: as each pipeline returns, land and record that node from the main context (steps
2.4–2.6), then claim again (step 3) and start pipelines for the new rows.

**Fallback** (no Workflow tool in this session): one background subagent call per agent, with the
review batching of step 2.3. When several nodes become ready at once, dispatch them all in a single
message — never one per message, which is exactly the serial behavior this plugin replaces.

## Step 2: One node's pipeline

Every claimed node runs this pipeline on its own — implement → review → land → record — and different
nodes are at different steps at the same time. Handle each completion the moment it arrives — the one
deliberate hold is step 2.3's review batching, which briefly waits out in-flight siblings to dispatch
one reviewer for several nodes.

1. **CLAIM.**

   ```
   relate query --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/dispatch.cypher
   ```

   It moves every pending node whose dependencies are all completed or cancelled to `in_progress` and
   prints one routing row per claimed node: `slug`, `type`, `model_tier`, `failure_policy`, `review`
   (`reviewer` when unset). That is all you need — agents read the rest themselves. **No rows** →
   nothing newly ready (step 3).

2. **IMPLEMENT.** A `code`/`test`/`chore` node first gets its own worktree (`research`/`decision`/`verify`
   nodes edit no files and get none) — identified by its branch, `gbuild/<feature>/<slug>`, wherever
   it lives, and idempotent, so a reset or re-dispatched node keeps its earlier work:

   ```
   git worktree list --porcelain | grep -q "branch refs/heads/gbuild/<feature>/<slug>$" \
     || git worktree add WT/<slug> gbuild/<feature>/<slug> 2>/dev/null \
     || git worktree add WT/<slug> -b gbuild/<feature>/<slug> BRANCH
   ```

   (reuse the registered worktree on that branch; else attach the branch an earlier attempt left; else
   fork a fresh one off `BRANCH` — nothing is redone. Create it where the step-0 placement rule puts
   node worktrees — `WT/<slug>` is the default, a harness convention overrides it.) Then dispatch the
   implementer — `Agent` tool, `subagent_type`
   `gbuild-implementer` / `gbuild-reviewer` (`gbuild:`-prefixed when namespaced), description
   `implement <slug>` / `review <slug>`, `run_in_background: true` — with this one prompt for both
   agents:

   ```
   gbuild node `<slug>`. Store: <DB>. Worktree: <worktree>. Feature branch: <BRANCH>. Agent file: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/agents/gbuild-<implementer|reviewer>.md.
   ```

   A step-2.3 review batch dispatches one reviewer with several of these lines, one per node — same
   format, nothing else appended. `<DB>`, `<BRANCH>` are `DB`, `BRANCH`; `<implementer|reviewer>` names
   the agent; `<worktree>` is the node's worktree for `code`/`test`/`chore` and `FT` (read-only)
   otherwise — every path absolute. The implementer gets a model per its `model_tier` and the reviewer
   per the same tier where the harness offers one
   (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/cost-model.md`).
   Append nothing — no acceptance, inputs, outputs, notes, failed criteria or agent-file text. Retries,
   repairs and fallbacks use the same prompt: the agent's brief carries the failed criteria.

3. **REVIEW — a fresh reviewer, or no reviewer at all.** The implementer replies with one line; read
   nothing else:
   - `failed <slug>: <reason>` → no review at any tier; record a fail:
     `["implementer failed: <reason>"]`.
   - `done <slug>` but no file → no review at any tier; record a fail:
     `["implementer reported done but <slug>.json is missing"]`.
   - `done <slug>` and `test -s INBOX/<slug>.json` → the node's `review` tier (its dispatch row)
     decides:
     - **`mechanical`** — no reviewer agent; you are the gate. Run the mechanical check yourself:

       ```
       relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl --param 'slug="<slug>"' \
         --fetch-params result=INBOX/<slug>.json < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/check-result.cypher
       ```

       `missing_outputs`, `invalid_outputs` and `unknown_outputs` all `[]` → verdict `pass`. Any name
       listed → verdict `fail`, one criterion per name: `missing output value: <name>`,
       `invalid output value: <name>`, `unknown output: <name>`. Exit 1 (the file is missing or not
       valid JSON) → verdict `fail`,
       `["result file rejected by the mechanical gate: <stderr, first 120 chars>"]`. Either way go
       straight to record (step 2.5); a fail goes on to the node's `failure_policy` (step 2.6).
     - **`reviewer`** — a fresh `gbuild-reviewer` agent, never the implementer. `cheap` nodes batch:
       hold a finished implementation while other `reviewer`-tier, `cheap` implementers are still in
       flight, and dispatch one reviewer covering every held node — up to 4 — as soon as none is left
       in flight. Never hold a node when nothing batchable is in flight, and never let one dragging
       implementer stall the rest: if several completions have arrived since a node finished, dispatch
       without the straggler. `strong` nodes never wait — their reviewer is dispatched alone, right
       away.

   The reviewer replies one block per node, every line prefixed `<slug>: `. A node passes only with a
   line exactly `<slug>: VERDICT: pass` and no `<slug>: [fail]` line for it; on
   `<slug>: VERDICT: fail`, `failed_criteria` is the text after `[fail] ` on each of its
   `<slug>: [fail] <criterion> — <reason>` lines, verbatim and in order. A dispatched slug with no
   verdict block → re-dispatch a reviewer for just that slug once, in the foreground (no background
   flag); still none → record a fail: `["reviewer returned no verdict"]` — the other nodes in the
   batch proceed on their own verdicts. A `<slug>: [fail] CONTRADICTS <upstream-slug>` line also hands
   that upstream node to its own `failure_policy` (step 2.6). The verdict comes only from this reply —
   never from `INBOX/<slug>.review.json` (which a pass doesn't even write).

4. **LAND.** A `pass` on a `code`/`test`/`chore` node merges its branch into the feature worktree `FT`,
   never the user's checkout — one merge at a time, never two in parallel:

   ```
   git -C FT merge --no-ff gbuild/<feature>/<slug>
   ```

   A conflict means two supposedly independent nodes touched the same lines: list them
   (`git -C FT diff --name-only --diff-filter=U`), `git -C FT merge --abort`, and record a fail instead:
   `["merge conflict with BRANCH in <path>[, <path>] — rebase gbuild/<feature>/<slug> onto BRANCH and resolve"]`.

5. **RECORD** — one call per node, as soon as its verdict is settled:

   ```
   relate query --database DB --mode jsonl \
     --param 'verdict={"slug":"<slug>","verdict":"pass","failed_criteria":[]}' \
     --fetch-params result=INBOX/<slug>.json --fetch-params review=INBOX/<slug>.review.json \
     < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/record.cypher
   ```

   `verdict` is all you type: `pass`, or `fail` with `failed_criteria` — the reviewer's `[fail]` lines
   or one of the fixed lines in steps 2.3–2.4, never your own words. Bind `result` from its file only on
   a pass (`--param 'result={}'` on every fail), and `review` from its file whenever `test -s` finds it
   — the reviewer writes one only on a fail and a `mechanical` node never does, so a pass usually
   binds `--param 'review={}'` — all three are always bound. record.cypher takes the outputs, times,
   notes and symbols from the file itself.

   No row, or another slug → it wasn't recorded (the node wasn't `in_progress`) — find out why. Exit 1
   or 6 → re-run once with `--param 'review={}'`; still failing → re-run with `--param 'result={}'
   --param 'review={}'` and verdict `fail`,
   `["result file rejected by record.cypher: <error.kind>: <error.message, first 120 chars>"]`, which
   can't fail. Then `rm -f INBOX/<slug>.*` and:
   - `completed: true` → for a worktree'd node `git worktree remove --force` its worktree (the path step 2.2 resolved) and
     `git branch -d gbuild/<feature>/<slug>` — only now, so a pass downgraded after its merge repairs in
     place. Non-empty `unselected` (a router's unchosen branches) → cancel them with
     `set-status.cypher`. Then claim again (step 3).
   - `completed: false` (a failed review, a merge conflict, a failed implementer, or a pass downgraded
     because `missing_outputs` is non-empty) → step 2.6.

6. **FAILURES.** Apply the node's `failure_policy` (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/failure-policies.md`),
   using its `attempt` as the count:
   - `retry` / `repair` → back to step 2.2 with the same prompt, reusing the node's existing worktree
     and branch — the next attempt builds on them, it does not start over. Bounded: 2 attempts.
   - `fallback` → remove the failed attempt's worktree and branch first (`git worktree remove --force`,
     `git branch -D`), then step 2.2 — a fresh branch off `BRANCH`; the brief names the alternate
     approach.
   - `skip` → `cancelled`; `escalate` (or an exhausted retry/repair) → `failed`, its dependents stay
     blocked while everything else keeps going; `stop` → `failed` and halt the run. Set it with
     `set-status.cypher`, then clean up a worktree'd node: `git worktree remove --force` its worktree and
     `git branch -D gbuild/<feature>/<slug>` — its work was never accepted, so it never lands.

   Then claim again (step 3) — except after `stop`: claim nothing more, finish the pipelines in flight,
   then step 4.

## Step 3: Claim again

After every `record.cypher` and `set-status.cypher` call, run dispatch.cypher (step 2.1) again and start
step 2.2 for every row it returns. That is the dataflow: a node starts the moment its own dependencies
complete, while unrelated slower nodes are still running. Between claims, wait for completion
notifications and handle each as it arrives.

A node is claimed only once everything it depends on has completed, so nodes in flight together never
read each other's outputs, and every file-touching node works in its own worktree — concurrency is safe
by construction. Your store calls and the merges into `FT` are the only serialized points; `FT` belongs
to this feature alone, so no other checkout can race them.

**Lost notifications.** Claude Code can drop a completion notification when 3 or more background agents
run at once. When an agent stays silent well past ones started after it, or you wake with nothing new to
handle, check instead of waiting: an implementer whose `INBOX/<slug>.json` exists counts as
`done <slug>` (it writes `.tmp` then renames, so presence means complete); otherwise, and for a
reviewer, fetch the reply by task id (`TaskOutput`) where the harness offers it. A reviewer whose reply
still can't be had is re-dispatched once in the foreground (step 2.3). Never take a verdict from a file.

Stop when a claim returns no rows and no agent is in flight: step 4.

## Step 4: Report and stop

```
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/progress.cypher
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/attention.cypher
```

Every `progress` row with `open: []` → the graph is done. Otherwise `attention` names what's stuck
(`failed` nodes with their last failed criteria, and what they block).

Report: which nodes ran this invocation, which passed review outright vs. needed a repair pass, and any
`failed` nodes needing a decision. Close with the next step:

- **Graph fully done** → say so plainly, then `next: /gbuild:review <feature>` — the per-node reviews
  graded each node against its own contract; nothing has yet looked at what the accumulated diff did to
  the codebase.
- **Work remains** (nodes `failed` awaiting a decision) → `next: /gbuild:status <feature>`.

## Resuming

Re-invoking `/gbuild:run <feature>` after an interruption re-runs step 0 fresh: the feature worktree is
resolved or re-attached, nodes an interrupted run left `in_progress` are reset (their worktrees and any
commits on their branches survive — the re-dispatch reuses them; their inbox files are discarded), and
the next claim picks up exactly the remaining frontier. Nothing needs to be told what already finished —
the store is the memory.

description: Reports a gbuild feature's graph — frontier, blocked, in-flight, completed, each node's review verdict, and the cluster shapes with evidence of what actually ran concurrently. Use to check progress or diagnose a stuck run.
---

Report status for `$ARGUMENTS`. This skill only reads the store. `DB` below is the feature's store:
`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/db`, beside the feature worktree `FT` at
`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/tree` — machine-local, never committed (a gbuild ≤ 0.7.1 store needs the
move in `reference/cypher.md`). Status never creates or attaches worktrees — if the store is missing,
the feature is gone (or was never charted here); say so.

## Store rules

- `relate --version` first. If it's missing or older than 1.0.1, stop: gbuild needs it
  (`curl -sSfL https://relatedb.ai/install.sh | bash`, or `relate upgrade`).
- One `relate` command at a time — never parallel tool calls on the same store.
- Always `--read-only`: status never writes, and a missing store fails fast instead of being created.
  It takes no lock, so it reads beside a running `/gbuild:run`.
- Always `--mode jsonl`, never `--timings`: one JSON object per row and nothing else — zero rows
  print nothing, so no output = no rows (`--timings` would append a telemetry line that is not a row).
- Any error: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/reference/cypher.md`.

## Mode

| arguments         | mode                                  |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| empty              | every feature store                    |
| a feature slug     | that feature only                      |

## Single feature

This is the human-facing report, so it's the one place that reads every node.

### 1. Load

```
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/status.cypher
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/validate.cypher
```

One call after the other. `status.cypher` gives one row per node with its derived `state`
(`frontier` / `blocked` / `in_progress` / `completed` / `cancelled` / `failed`), `wave`, `waiting_on`,
review summary, timestamps and `last_dependency_at` — don't re-derive any of these by hand.

### 2. Render the graph

Draw the DAG with a marker per node state:

```
✓ completed   ◐ in_progress   ○ frontier   ● blocked   ✗ failed   – cancelled
```

Annotate blocked nodes with what they're waiting on (`waiting_on`):
`● d-join-and-sum ← b-consume-doubled, c-consume-squared`.

Group by `wave` so fan-out is visible in the layout, not just in the dependency list.

### 3. Review verdicts

For every `completed` node, one line: passed outright (`review_attempts: 1`), or passed after N repair
attempts. For `failed` nodes, `last_failed_criteria` verbatim — this is what a human needs to make the
`escalate`/`stop` call.

### 4. Concurrency evidence

`run` schedules as dataflow: a node is claimed the moment its last dependency completes, not when its
wave does. Nodes sharing a `wave` need not overlap — a short chain can finish before a slow node beside
it — so don't judge by overlap; check dispatch timing instead, from the `status.cypher` rows of step 1.

For each node with both `started_at` and `last_dependency_at` (the latest `completed_at` among its
completed dependencies), report the gap from `last_dependency_at` to `started_at`. A few minutes is
the dependency's review, merge and record — dataflow working. A much longer gap, e.g. a start that
waited for an unrelated slower node to complete, means the node sat ready while something else held it
back (`run` driven wave by wave, or a lost completion notification) — a bug in how `run` was driven,
not a graph problem. A node with repair attempts (`review_attempts` > 1) started late by design: its
times are the passing attempt's. Nodes with no dependencies should have started together at the
beginning of the run.

### 5. Next action

One priority-ordered list: what `/gbuild:run <feature>` would do next (the current frontier), and
anything needing a human decision first (`failed` nodes, an empty frontier with incomplete nodes
remaining, `in_progress` nodes when no run is active — interrupted work `run` will reset).

### 6. Invariant checks

`validate.cypher` is the invariant check — it covers non-empty acceptance, acceptance coverage,
acyclicity, completed nodes without a passing review or missing an output value, orphan chores, and the
`FROM` cut test. Report every row it returned, numbered. If it returned nothing, say so in one line —
don't let silence be ambiguous between "checked, clear" and "not checked."

## All-features mode

Don't read every node of every feature. For each store found — `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/*/db` — one

# gbuild — Claude Code + OpenCode plugin

Graph-native task planning and execution: design a feature with the human, plan it as a real
dependency graph, then run it with actual concurrent fan-out, a dedicated review pass on every node,
and durable per-node checkpoints.

## The workflow

Design the feature first — `/gbuild:design` when the work needs shaping before it can be charted,
conversation (your agent's normal plan mode) when it doesn't — then hand it to gbuild:

1. `/gbuild:design <the feature>` — shape it with the human into committed design artifacts (`docs/design/<slug>/`) on the feature branch in its own worktree; it ends only when you call the design good, and re-invoking with the slug resumes from the commits
2. `/gbuild:plan <the plan>` — chart it as a dependency graph
3. `/gbuild:run <slug>` — run it, once; it starts each node the moment its dependencies complete, until the graph completes (re-invoke only to resume an interrupted run)
4. `/gbuild:review <slug>` — audit the accumulated branch
5. Issues? `/gbuild:plan <slug> --add "<fix>"`, then `/gbuild:run` again. Clean? `/gbuild:pr <slug>`
6. `/gbuild:cleanup <slug>` — once the PR is merged (or the feature is abandoned), reclaim its whole local footprint: the worktrees it opened, its branches, the store

The feature branch lives in its own git worktree (created by `design` or `plan`) — your checkout never changes
branches, your uncommitted work is never in the way, and several features can be in flight in parallel
without racing each other's `HEAD`.

(OpenCode: `/gbuild-plan`, `/gbuild-run`, … — same loop.)

Inspired by the graph-engineering thread at
[x.com/0xwhrrari/status/2086784668003598356](https://x.com/0xwhrrari/status/2086784668003598356):
sequence isn't dependency, every node needs an explicit contract, edges carry data not just order, and
verification never grades itself.

## Install

gbuild needs the `relate` CLI on PATH — see [Runtime](#runtime).

```bash
claude plugin install gbuild@oskars.ai
```

For local development:

```bash
claude --plugin-dir ./plugins/gbuild
```

### OpenCode

The same directory is also an OpenCode (V2) plugin, published to npm as
[`opencode-gbuild`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/opencode-gbuild) — `index.ts` registers the seven
skills and seven slash commands (`/gbuild-design`, `/gbuild-plan`, `/gbuild-run`, `/gbuild-status`,
`/gbuild-review`, `/gbuild-pr`, `/gbuild-cleanup`) from the same markdown the Claude plugin uses.

```bash
opencode plugin add opencode-gbuild
```

`opencode plugin update opencode-gbuild` moves to the latest published version. For local
