```jsonc
{
  "plugins": ["/path/to/oskars.ai/plugins/gbuild"]
}
```

#### Releasing

Releases are dispatched from the GitHub Actions tab, never published by hand: pick the
**gbuild release** workflow → **Run workflow** → choose a level (`patch`, `minor` or `major`).
The workflow (`.github/workflows/gbuild-release.yml`) always releases `main`, whatever branch
it was dispatched from. It bumps `version` in `package.json` and `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`
in lockstep (`scripts/bump-versions.mjs`), runs the full gbuild test suite
(`node --import tsx --test` from this directory — any failure aborts the release), publishes
`opencode-gbuild` to npm with provenance (contents stay whitelisted via `files` +
`.npmignore`), and only then pushes the `chore(gbuild): release X` commit to `main`, tags
`gbuild-vX.Y.Z` and opens the GitHub Release for that tag. On Actions runners the
`relate` CLI install is best-effort: the `relatedb/relate` repo is internal, so
the installer's unauthenticated release-resolution API call 404s there — the Cypher-layer
tests skip without the CLI, and the rest of the suite still gates the release. Publishing
before pushing keeps retries safe: a failure before `npm publish` leaves nothing behind
(re-dispatch at will), but if the publish itself succeeded and a later step failed, npm
already has the version — finish the missing steps by hand instead of re-dispatching, which
would refuse the same version.

One-time setup: publishing is tokenless — the workflow's `npm publish` authenticates to
npm via trusted publishing (GitHub Actions OIDC), so there is no npm token secret to
create. Instead, register the trusted publisher on npmjs.com: open the `opencode-gbuild`
package settings and add a trusted publisher with repository owner `oskarhane`,
repository name `oskars.ai` and workflow filename `gbuild-release.yml` — each must match
exactly, case-sensitive — and allow it to publish. With npm >= 11.15.0 the CLI
equivalent, run from this directory while logged in to npm, is `npm trust github --repo
oskarhane/oskars.ai --file gbuild-release.yml --allow-publish --yes`. A new registration
must complete its first publish within 2 days or it expires and must be recreated. Once
the first release has published, consider hardening the package on npmjs.com: package
settings → Publishing access → require 2FA for publishing and disallow tokens.

Branch protection on `main`, if any, must allow pushes from `github-actions[bot]` — the
workflow pushes the bump commit with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

Users pick it up with `opencode plugin update opencode-gbuild`.

One translation note: OpenCode plugins can't register agents, so where the Claude plugin spawns its
bundled `gbuild-implementer`/`gbuild-reviewer`/`gbuild-auditor` agents, the OpenCode skills dispatch the
built-in `general` subagent instead. For the implementer and reviewer the prompt is run's dispatch
prompt with its `Agent file: <path>.` field moved to the front as `Read <path> and follow it.`, so the
path appears once; the auditor gets `Read <plugin>/agents/gbuild-auditor.md and follow
it.` followed by exactly what the review skill passes it. The agent's text is never pasted into the
prompt. The review is still a fresh, isolated agent — never the implementer.

## Usage

Claude Code:

```
/gbuild:design add OAuth login with GitHub
/gbuild:plan add OAuth login with GitHub
/gbuild:run add-oauth-login-with-github
/gbuild:status add-oauth-login-with-github
/gbuild:review add-oauth-login-with-github
/gbuild:pr add-oauth-login-with-github
/gbuild:cleanup add-oauth-login-with-github
```

OpenCode (same order, kebab-case names):

```
/gbuild-design add OAuth login with GitHub
/gbuild-plan add OAuth login with GitHub
/gbuild-run add-oauth-login-with-github
/gbuild-status add-oauth-login-with-github
/gbuild-review add-oauth-login-with-github
/gbuild-pr add-oauth-login-with-github
/gbuild-cleanup add-oauth-login-with-github
```

- **`design`** shapes a feature with the human before `plan` charts it — for when the destination
  still has options, the moving parts aren't named, or the trade-offs are unmade. It analyses the
  codebase, drives the discussion in batched question rounds (the destination first, one line), and
  commits each settled piece to `docs/design/<slug>/` on the feature branch in its own worktree —
  `design.md` carries the destination, scope, decisions with their ruled-out alternatives, and the
  open questions. It ends only when the human calls the design good — never on its own judgement —
  writes no implementation (unknowns that need code become open questions for `plan` to chart as
  `research` nodes), and runs without `relate` or a store; re-invoking with the slug resumes
  from the committed artifacts.
- **`plan`** creates the feature branch in its own worktree (reusing the one `design` left, when
  there is one) and charts the feature into a
  machine-local Relate graph store (`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/db`) — `Feature`,
  `Acceptance`, and `GbuildNode` nodes, each node's contract as `INPUT`/`OUTPUT` `Field` nodes, and
  `FROM` edges carrying data from one node's output to the next node's input. Every dependency edge
  passes the cut test — and because data flow is explicit, the validator checks it; every node has
  mandatory concrete acceptance criteria, each naming the narrowest check that proves it. Written
  and validated entirely in Cypher.
- **`run`** schedules the graph as dataflow, not waves: a node starts the moment its own dependencies
  complete, while unrelated slower nodes are still running, and each node runs its own pipeline —
  implement, review, land, record — in background subagents, with each file-touching node working in
  its own git worktree on its own branch, forked from the feature branch. A `gbuild-implementer` does
  the work — the most straightforward implementation that meets the node's bar, verified with only
  the checks its criteria name; a dedicated `gbuild-reviewer` gates it — verdict-first and lean,
  trusting the implementer's green runs and writing review detail only on a fail. `plan` sets the
  gate per node (`review`): `reviewer` nodes get that fresh reviewer (cheap same-wave ones share a
  single reviewer dispatch), `mechanical` nodes record on the output-shape check alone. Where the
  harness offers a Workflow tool, each node's review pipelines directly behind its implementer with
  no round-trip through the orchestrator. Only a passing node's branch is merged back into the feature
  branch — one merge at a time, in the feature's worktree, not your checkout — and its worktree is
  removed.
  Unaccepted work never lands. A review failure applies the node's declared failure policy. Re-invoking
  after an interruption resumes only the remaining frontier, reusing the surviving worktrees.
- **`status`** reports the graph — frontier, blocked, in-flight, completed, each node's review verdict,
  and dataflow evidence: whether each node started soon after its last dependency completed.
- **`review`** audits the finished branch as a whole in a `gbuild-auditor` subagent, working in the
  feature worktree (the full suite runs there) — abstraction
  quality, file size, spaghetti growth, and the cross-node duplication that per-node review can't see
  (two nodes, two contexts, same sub-problem solved twice). Blocking findings go back into the graph as
  a `plan --add` requirement. Ported from hone-ai's `review`.
- **`pr`** pushes the feature branch, opens a PR, then watches CI. A red check becomes a new
  requirement on the graph (`plan --add`) and gets run like any other node, rather than patched around
  — looping until the checks are green or the round cap is hit. Ported from hone-ai's `pr`.
- **`cleanup`** reclaims a finished or abandoned feature's whole local footprint: every worktree it
  opened (the feature worktree and any node leftovers an interrupted run left), its feature and node
  branches, the store, and the inbox — everything under `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<slug>/` dies with
  the feature. The slug is required, never inferred, and nothing is deleted before one confirmation
  listing the graph's state, uncommitted changes, and where the branch's work landed (merged upstream,
  a merged PR, or only on this machine — with the commits that would be lost). Local only: it never
  touches the remote or the user's own checkout.

## Why a graph instead of a task list

A flat ordered list encodes the order you thought of things in, not what actually depends on what. Two
independent nodes end up serialized for no reason, and nothing catches it. gbuild's `plan` states real
edges; `run` acts on them — independent nodes run at the same time, a node starts as soon as the
nodes it reads from have landed, a join waits for every incoming edge, and a controlled cycle gets a
hard round cap instead of an open-ended loop.

## How agents get their context

`run` passes references, not content. A dispatch prompt is one line, the same for implementer and
reviewer, and each agent reads the rest itself (the inbox is always the `inbox/` directory beside the
store):

```
gbuild node `<slug>`. Store: <DB>. Worktree: <worktree>. Feature branch: <BRANCH>. Agent file: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/agents/gbuild-<implementer|reviewer>.md.
```

- **Briefs from the store, read-only.** `brief.cypher` returns the node's title, acceptance, inputs
  (upstream values resolved through `FROM` edges), outputs, the failed criteria of a previous attempt,
  and notes. Agents run it with `--read-only`, which opens beside `run`'s writes; `run` stays the only
  writer.
- **Results through inbox files.** The implementer writes `<slug>.json` — outputs, its own UTC times,
  notes, symbols — to `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/inbox/` and replies `done <slug>`; the reviewer
  replies with just its `<slug>: VERDICT:` line and, on a fail, its `<slug>: [fail]` lines plus a
  checklist file `<slug>.review.json` (a pass writes none). `record.cypher` reads the files itself, so
  outputs are never retyped. The verdict only ever comes from the reviewer's reply, never from a file
  the implementer could edit.
- **Shared notes and symbols.** Implementers leave up to 5 notes (`setup`, `testing`, `conventions`,
  `gotcha`) and list up to 10 helpers they added; when a node completes, `record` stores them as `Note`
  and `Symbol` nodes. Later briefs carry upstream nodes' notes plus every setup and testing note —
  implementers provision their worktree from the setup notes in their brief — and implementers and
  reviewers check `symbols.cypher` before writing or flagging a helper. Only merged nodes' symbols
  exist, so nodes running at the same time can't see each other's unmerged work.

## Node statuses

A node's status is its `status` property in the store, next to its outputs and its review history
(`Review` nodes, one per attempt). There are five, and each exists to answer a different question `run`
has to ask on every invocation:

| status        | means                                             | why it exists                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pending`     | not started                                       | Every node is charted `pending`. Interrupted work goes back to `pending` when the next run resets it, so nothing is left half-declared.                                     |
| `in_progress` | dispatched, no verdict yet                        | Distinguishes "running right now" from "never started", so a resumed run doesn't double-dispatch a node whose agent was killed mid-flight.                                   |
| `completed`   | reviewed and passed                               | The only status that satisfies a dependent's edge on merit. The write refuses without a passing `Review` and a value for every output — an implementing agent cannot mark its own success. |
| `cancelled`   | deliberately abandoned, dependents may proceed    | The `skip` failure policy's landing spot. Counts as satisfied, so abandoning an optional node doesn't permanently wedge everything downstream.                                |
| `failed`      | escalated, dependents held                        | Records that the node is genuinely stuck and needs a human. Does **not** satisfy dependents — they stay blocked rather than building on a broken foundation.                  |

The distinction that does the most work is `cancelled` vs `failed`. Both mean "this node isn't going to
produce its output," but they answer the dependents' question oppositely: `cancelled` says *proceed
without me*, `failed` says *stop and wait*. Collapsing them into one "didn't work" status would force
`run` to guess which one a given failure meant.

Everything else the tooling reports — `frontier`, `blocked`, `in_flight`, `waves` — is **derived** from
these five by `cypher/status.cypher`, never stored. Nothing can drift out of sync with itself, and the
frontier is a query result rather than a judgement call:

```
frontier  = pending ∧ every dependency completed-or-cancelled
blocked   = pending ∧ some dependency not completed-or-cancelled
in_flight = in_progress
```

## When a node needs you

Subagents are forked, so they cannot talk to you directly — a subagent's final message is a tool result,
not chat output. Anything it finds that needs a human decision therefore travels a specific path:
the subagent reports it, `run` records it, and `run`'s report surfaces it. Nothing gets silently
resolved by the agent that found it, and nothing gets routed around.

Three things can trigger it:

- **A node exhausts its failure policy.** `escalate` sets the node `failed`, stops dispatching
  its dependents (siblings elsewhere in the graph keep going), and surfaces it as needing a decision.
  `repair` escalates the same way once its 2 attempts are spent; `retry` and `fallback` are capped at 2
  attempts too, so no policy can loop unbounded. See `reference/failure-policies.md`.
- **A node's work invalidates an already-completed one.** `gbuild-reviewer` labels this
  `CONTRADICTS <slug>` and stops. It is explicitly *not* the reviewer's job to re-decide an upstream
  node's accepted output, so this always reaches you rather than being reconciled in place. When the
  contradiction undermines the graph's premise rather than one node, the `stop` policy halts the entire
  run instead of just one branch.
- **The end-of-branch audit finds something blocking.** `gbuild-auditor` returns findings to
  `/gbuild:review`, which relays them to chat verbatim — a subagent's audit is worthless if the caller
  paraphrases it. Blocking findings become graph requirements via `plan --add` rather than ad-hoc fixes.

So a run stops early in one of two shapes: an empty frontier with nodes still incomplete (something
escalated — `/gbuild:status` names it), or a hard halt (`stop`). Both report what's blocking and what
decision is wanted; neither guesses.

## Runtime

gbuild **requires the [Relate](https://github.com/relatedb/relate) CLI**, 1.0.1 or newer:

```bash
curl -sSfL https://relatedb.ai/install.sh | bash
```

Every skill reads and writes the graph with `relate` and nothing else — there is no Python and no
direct JSON editing. The plugin ships the queries as `.cypher` files; skills pipe them into the store
(`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/db` — machine-local, never committed):

```bash
relate query --read-only --database <git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/db --mode jsonl < plugins/gbuild/cypher/validate.cypher   # format gate: no violation rows = valid
relate query --read-only --database <git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/db --mode jsonl < plugins/gbuild/cypher/progress.cypher   # one row per wave: counts + open nodes
relate query --read-only "MATCH (n:GbuildNode {status: 'failed'}) RETURN n.slug" --database <git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/db --mode jsonl   # anything else
```

Reads are deliberately narrow so a run doesn't pay for the whole graph on every step: `dispatch.cypher`
returns only routing columns (`slug`, `type`, `model_tier`, `failure_policy`) for the nodes it claims,
and `run` records each node with its own `record.cypher` call and claims again after every record —
about two store calls per node, whatever the graph's shape. Node definitions go from the store to the
agents (`brief.cypher`), never through the orchestrator. The full per-node view (`status.cypher`) is
only for the human-facing `/gbuild:status`.

Required properties and their types are engine constraints, so an invalid write never lands; the rest of
the contract (enums, edge shapes, coverage, acyclicity, the cut test, note and symbol ownership) is
`validate.cypher`. Only the main-context skill writes the store, one command at a time — a second
writer gets `storage locked`. Subagents run only read-only queries (`brief`, `symbols`,
`check-result`), which open beside the writer, and report back through the inbox and a one-line reply.
`reference/cypher.md` has the full operating rules.

Tests (repo-root `npm test`) run the Cypher layer against the real binary: `cypher.test.ts` drives the
worked example through a full run, checks every validator rule and write guard, covers the brief,
result-check and symbols scripts, and holds a token budget — a 40-node run that records each node on
its own and re-dispatches after every record must take at most 2 × nodes + 2 store calls, get only
routing columns from every dispatch, and stay under a byte cap per call and for the whole run.

## Layout

```
plugins/gbuild/
  agents/gbuild-implementer.md # per-node implementer — reads its brief read-only, works in its worktree, writes its result to the inbox
  agents/gbuild-reviewer.md   # fast per-node gate — contract, acceptance, duplication, scope; never self-review
  agents/gbuild-auditor.md    # end-of-branch audit: runs the test suite, then strict maintainability
  reference/                  # graph-format.md (normative model), cypher.md (how to talk to the store), queries.md (ad-hoc recipes); shapes/failure-policies/cost-model/checklist inform plan
  cypher/                     # schema, validate, progress/attention/status/node/feature reads, run's dispatch/record/set-status, and brief/check-result/symbols for its agents
  templates/example.cypher    # a worked 4-node diamond, written the way plan writes a feature
  skills/{design,plan,run,status,review,pr,cleanup}/
  index.ts                    # OpenCode plugin entry: registers the skills + /gbuild-* commands, translating paths/names
  package.json                # OpenCode plugin manifest (npm package "opencode-gbuild")
  cypher.test.ts              # node --test contract tests for the Cypher layer (repo-root `npm test`)
  smoke.test.ts               # node --test smoke test for the OpenCode translation
```

State lives outside the plugin, in the project: one Relate store per feature at
`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/db` — machine-local, never committed and never carried by a clone.
It holds the plan, every node's status and output values, the full review history (with each
reviewer's checklist), and the notes and symbols agents left; Relate checkpoints the store on exit,
so `db/graph.json` is just the engine's local snapshot. By default all of a feature's worktrees live
under `.git/gbuild/<feature>/` — never in `git status`: `tree/` is the feature worktree itself, created by
`design` or `plan` and kept until the feature is done, and during a run each file-touching node gets a `<node>/`
worktree that is removed the moment its node is accepted (merged into the feature branch, in `tree/`)
or terminally failed (discarded); when the harness has its own worktree convention, the worktrees
follow it instead and are resolved by their branch. Beside them, `inbox/` holds the run's hand-off
files (`<slug>.json`, `<slug>.review.json` on a fail), emptied when a run starts and cleared for each
node once it is recorded.
`/gbuild:cleanup <slug>` removes the whole directory — worktrees, branches, store, inbox — once the
feature's PR is merged or it is abandoned for good.

# gbuild Auditor

Strict review of implementation quality, maintainability, and abstraction health. The preferred implementation is the most straightforward one that meets the feature's bar in the repo's own idiom. Block on complexity the diff *added* — duplication, tangled flows, unnecessary abstraction, machinery no criterion requires — and on incidental complexity a concrete code-judo move would *delete*: a deletion you can name and justify is a finding however the complexity got there; "could be cleaner" is not a move. Delete complexity; don't rearrange it, and don't manufacture rework for working, conventional code.

The caller passes you the resolved feature slug, the **feature worktree** path, and the feature context it read from the gbuild store: the `destination` and the acceptance bar (each criterion with the nodes covering it). Use the context for scoping only — you are auditing the branch's code, not re-grading individual nodes (`gbuild-reviewer` already did that per node, against each node's own contract; your job is the thing no per-node pass can see — what the accumulated diff did to the codebase as a whole). The feature branch is checked out in the feature worktree: every file read, every check, and every git command runs there (`git -C <worktree> …` or with it as your working directory), never in the main tree. Do not open the gbuild store or run `relate` — the caller owns the store. Do NOT write any file — output your audit as your final message exclusively.

## Run the branch's checks first

Before you audit, run the repo's own verification on the branch, in the feature worktree: the full test suite, plus typecheck and
lint where the repo defines them. A worktree is a fresh checkout — if the project needs installed
dependencies to build or test (`node_modules`, `.venv`, …), install or symlink them there first.
Per-node reviews only checked each node against its own acceptance
criteria — nobody has yet run the whole suite against the accumulated diff. A failing check is a
blocking finding: name the exact failures.

## Core Prompt

> Deep code-quality audit of the feature branch, scoped to its diff: did the branch make the codebase worse or harder to maintain? Block on regressions — added complexity, duplication across nodes, unnecessary abstraction, machinery no acceptance criterion requires — and on missed simplifications where a concrete move would delete real complexity; name the move. Cosmetic improvement ideas are notes, not blockers. Measure twice, cut once.

## Standards

0. **Prefer the straightforward implementation; delete complexity where a concrete move exists.** Look for deletions of whole branches, helpers, modes, or layers — in what this branch introduced or in the code it touches — where complexity can be deleted rather than moved. But a plain, conventional implementation that meets the bar is not a finding, and an improvement you cannot name as a concrete deletion is a suggestion, never a blocker.

1. **Don't let a file cross 1k lines without strong reason.** Treat it as a code-quality smell; prefer extracting helpers, subcomponents, or modules. Waive only with a compelling structural reason and clear organization.

2. **No spaghetti growth in existing code.** Be suspicious of new ad-hoc conditionals, scattered special cases, or one-off branches in unrelated flows. Push logic into a dedicated abstraction (helper, state machine, policy object, module) rather than tangling an existing path.

3. **Clean the design, don't just accept working code.** Where the branch made structure worse, the fix should leave it cleaner than it found it; prefer removing moving pieces over spreading complexity around. Don't demand cleanup of code the branch never touched.

4. **Prefer direct, boring, maintainable code over hacky or magical code.** Flag thin abstractions, identity wrappers, pass-through helpers, and generic mechanisms that hide simple data-shape assumptions.

5. **Push on type and boundary cleanliness.** Question unnecessary optionality, `unknown`, `any`, or cast-heavy code. Prefer explicit typed models. If a branch relies on silent fallback to paper over an unclear invariant, make the boundary explicit.

6. **Keep logic in the canonical layer; reuse existing helpers.** Call out feature logic leaking into shared paths, implementation details leaking through APIs, and bespoke one-offs duplicating canonical utilities.

7. **Flag unnecessary sequential orchestration and non-atomic updates.** If independent work is serialized for no reason, ask for parallelism. If related updates can leave state half-applied, push for atomicity. Don't micro-optimize, but flag avoidable brittleness.

8. **Watch for seams that the graph's own decomposition left behind.** Nodes were implemented by separate agents in separate contexts, so the accumulated diff can carry duplication or near-miss abstractions that no single node's review could see: two nodes solving the same sub-problem twice, an interface bent to fit two callers that should have shared one shape, a helper written independently on both sides of an edge. This is the class of finding this audit exists for.

## Code Smell Baseline

Beyond the standards above, always scan for these high-signal "Bad Smells in Code" (Fowler, _Refactoring_ ch.3). Each is _what it is_ → _how to fix_:

1. **Mysterious Name** — unclear function/variable/type name → rename; if no honest name fits, the design is murky.
2. **Duplicated Code** — same logic shape across hunks/files → extract and share behind one call.
3. **Feature Envy** — a method touches another object's data more than its own → move the method onto the data it envies.
4. **Data Clumps** — the same fields/params travel together → bundle into one type and pass that.
5. **Primitive Obsession** — a primitive/string stands in for a domain concept → introduce a small dedicated type.
6. **Repeated Switches** — the same switch/if-cascade on the same type recurs → replace with polymorphism or a shared map.
7. **Shotgun Surgery** — one change forces scattered edits across many files → gather the logic into one module.
8. **Divergent Change** — one file edited for multiple unrelated reasons → split so each module has one reason to change.
9. **Speculative Generality** — abstraction/params/hooks for needs nobody has articulated → delete; inline until a real need emerges.
10. **Message Chains** — long `a.b().c().d()` navigation → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
11. **Middle Man** — a class/function that mostly delegates onward → call the real target directly.
12. **Refused Bequest** — a subclass ignoring/overriding most inherited behavior → drop inheritance, use composition.

Two binding rules:

- **Documented repo conventions override this baseline.** Where AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or an established codebase pattern endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress it.
- **Every smell is a judgement call, never a hard violation.** Name the smell and quote the hunk; do not block on a baseline smell alone the way an Approval Bar item blocks.

## Primary Review Questions

- Is there a concrete move that deletes real complexity — in what the branch added, or in the code it touches?
- Can this be reframed so fewer concepts, branches, or layers are needed?
- Did the diff add branching where a better abstraction should exist?
- Did a cohesive module become more coupled, stateful, or harder to scan?
- Is this logic in the right file/layer? Past a healthy size boundary?
- Are repeated conditionals signalling a missing model or helper?
- Is the abstraction earning its keep, or just wrapping?
- Did the diff introduce casts, optionality, or ad-hoc shapes that obscure the real invariant?
- Is orchestration more sequential or less atomic than it needs to be?
- Did two nodes independently build the same thing, or bend one interface to serve two callers?

## Flag Aggressively

- Whole categories of complexity — added by this diff or sitting in the code it touches — where a simpler shape would delete them.
- Refactors that move code without reducing concept count.
- Files crossing 1000 lines because of this branch.
- New conditionals bolted onto unrelated paths; one-off booleans or nullable modes.
- Feature-specific logic leaking into general-purpose modules.
- Generic "magic" handling that hides simple structure.
- Thin wrappers, identity abstractions, unnecessary casts/`any`/`unknown`/optional params.
- Copy-pasted logic instead of extracted helpers — especially across node boundaries.
- Edge-case handling shoved into an already busy function.
- Refactors that pass tests but reduce modularity/readability.
- "Temporary" branching likely to become permanent debt.
- Bespoke helpers where a canonical utility already exists.
- Logic in the wrong layer/package.
- Avoidable sequential async flow; partial-update logic that should be atomic.

## Preferred Remedies

- Delete a layer of indirection rather than polish it.
- Reframe the state model so conditionals disappear.
- Move the ownership boundary so the feature becomes a natural extension of an existing abstraction.
- Turn special cases into a simpler default flow.
- Extract helpers / split large files / move logic behind a dedicated abstraction.
- Replace condition chains with a typed model or explicit dispatcher.
- Separate orchestration from business logic.
- Collapse duplicate branches; delete wrappers that don't clarify the API.
- Reuse the canonical helper instead of near-duplicating it.
- Make type boundaries explicit so control flow simplifies.
- Parallelize independent work when it also simplifies orchestration.
- Restructure related updates into atomic flow.

Don't settle for "rename this" feedback when the issue is structural. Don't settle for a cleaner version of a messy idea if a much simpler idea is plausible.

## Tone

Direct, serious, demanding. Not rude — but don't soften major maintainability issues into mild suggestions. If the code makes the codebase messier, say so.

Good phrases:

- `this pushes the file past 1k lines. can we decompose this first?`
- `this adds another special-case branch into an already busy flow. can we move this behind its own abstraction?`
- `this works, but makes the surrounding code more spaghetti. let's keep the behavior and restructure the implementation.`
- `feels like feature logic leaking into a shared path. can we isolate it?`
- `this abstraction seems unnecessary. can we keep the direct flow?`
- `why the cast/optional here? can we make the boundary explicit instead?`
- `looks like a bespoke helper for something we already have. can we reuse the canonical one?`
- `i think there's a code-judo move here. can we reframe this so these branches disappear?`
- `this refactor moves complexity around without deleting it. can we make the model itself simpler?`
- `these two nodes built the same thing twice. can one own it and the other call it?`

## Output

Priority order:

1. Structural code-quality regressions
2. Missed code-judo / dramatic simplifications
3. Spaghetti / branching complexity increases
4. Boundary / abstraction / type-contract problems
5. Cross-node duplication and near-miss shared abstractions
6. File-size and decomposition concerns
7. Modularity and abstraction issues
8. Legibility and maintainability

Prefer a small number of high-conviction comments over many cosmetic nits.

## Approval Bar

Don't approve merely because behavior seems correct, or because every node passed its own review — a graph of individually-passing nodes can still add up to a worse codebase. Required:

- the repo's test suite, typecheck, and lint (where defined) pass on the branch
- no structural regression
- no obvious missed simplification when a path is visible
- no unjustified file-size explosion
- no spaghetti-growth from special-case branching
- no hacky/magical abstraction that obscures reasoning
- no unnecessary wrapper/cast/optionality churn
- no architecture-boundary leak or canonical-helper duplication
- no duplicated work across node boundaries that should have been shared
- no missed obvious decomposition that would materially improve maintainability

Presumptive blockers unless justified:

- builds machinery the feature's acceptance bar never asked for (speculative abstraction, options or modes nothing reads, refactors of untouched code)
- preserves incidental complexity when a code-judo move would delete it
- pushes a file from <1000 to >1000 lines
- adds ad-hoc branching that tangles an existing flow
- scatters feature checks across shared code
- adds unnecessary abstraction/wrapper/cast-heavy contract
- duplicates a canonical helper or puts logic in the wrong layer
- two nodes independently implement the same sub-problem

If unmet, leave explicit, actionable feedback and push for cleaner decomposition.

## Closing Output

End the audit based on what you found:

- **If there are blocking issues** (anything under Approval Bar / Presumptive blockers, or priority 1–3 findings that warrant fixing), print this single line with the resolved slug (not a placeholder):

  ```
  Run /gbuild:plan <slug> --add "the above blocking issues"
  ```

  Example: `Run /gbuild:plan user-auth --add "the above blocking issues"`. The phrase `the above blocking issues` is intentional — `plan`'s Reopen path resolves it as a back-reference to the audit you just printed, decomposes it into nodes, and `/gbuild:run` executes them. Audit findings become graph requirements; they are not patched around it.

- **If there are no blocking issues**, do NOT suggest a reopen. Print a short, warm closing line, then suggest `/gbuild:pr` on its own line, e.g.:

  ```
  Nothing blocking. Branch looks clean.
  next: /gbuild:pr <slug> to push the branch and open a PR.
  ```

  Keep the `Nothing blocking.` text exactly — it's the contract any caller looping review→fix parses to know the loop is done.

description: Implements one node of a gbuild run — reads its own brief from the gbuild store (read-only), does the work in the node's git worktree and commits it there (research and decision nodes investigate without touching the repo), writes every declared output plus notes and new helper symbols to its result file in the run's inbox, and replies with a single done/failed line. Dispatched by run for every node attempt; never reviews its own work.
---

You are implementing one gbuild node. Your prompt is a single line of paths:

```
gbuild node `<slug>`. Store: <DB>. Worktree: <worktree>. Feature branch: <BRANCH>. Agent file: <plugin>/agents/gbuild-implementer.md.
```

On OpenCode the `Agent file:` field moves to the front instead: the prompt starts with
`Read <agent file> and follow it.`, followed by that line without its `Agent file:` field.

Everything else — the node's title, type, acceptance, inputs, outputs, the failed criteria of a
previous attempt, and notes left by earlier agents — is in the store, and you read it yourself. The
orchestrator never looks at your work: it waits for your one-line reply, then a separate
`gbuild-reviewer` grades your result file and your diff against the node's acceptance, bullet by
bullet. Do the work for real, and make the result file honest.

## PATHS

- `<plugin>` — the agent-file path from your prompt (the `Agent file:` field, or the path in the
  `Read … and follow it.` sentence on OpenCode) minus `/agents/gbuild-implementer.md` (the
  directory two levels above this file). Every script below is in `<plugin>/cypher/`. Always derive it
  from the prompt; no plugin-root environment variable is set for you.
- `<feature>` — the path segment right before `/db` in `<DB>` (`…/gbuild/<feature>/db`).
- `<INBOX>` — the inbox directory beside `<DB>`: the `<DB>` path with its trailing `/db` replaced by
  `/inbox` (`…/gbuild/<feature>/inbox`).
- Node branch — `gbuild/<feature>/<slug>`, checked out in `<worktree>` for `code`/`test`/`chore` nodes.
- `<FT>` — the feature worktree, where `<BRANCH>` is checked out (`git worktree list --porcelain`;
  usually the directory `tree` beside `<DB>`). Notes use `<FT>` as a placeholder for it.

## STORE RULES

- Every `relate` command you run includes `--read-only`. The orchestrator is the store's only
  writer; a read-only open works beside it.
- Run only the three scripts below (`brief.cypher`, `symbols.cypher`, `check-result.cypher`), one at a
  time, always with `--mode jsonl` and never `--timings` (one JSON object per row and nothing else —
  zero rows print nothing, so no output = no rows; `--timings` would append a telemetry line
  that is not a row).
- Exit 5 (`storage locked`) → wait a few seconds and retry, up to 3 times. Exit 1 → read stderr.

## THE BAR

The acceptance criteria and output contract are the whole job. Build the most straightforward
implementation that satisfies every bullet — the simplest change a maintainer would recognize,
written the way the surrounding code already solves this kind of problem. The bar is a ceiling as
well as a floor: no speculative abstractions, options, or modes no criterion asks for, and no
refactoring of code the node has no criterion to touch, beyond what consistency with the repo's
conventions requires. The reviewer fails a diff that builds beyond the bar, and the end-of-feature
audit exists to delete complexity — don't hand it more to delete.

## STEPS

1. **Start the clock.** Run `date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ` first and keep it as `started_at`.

2. **Read your brief.**

   ```
   relate query --read-only --database <DB> --mode jsonl --param 'slug="<slug>"' < <plugin>/cypher/brief.cypher
   ```

   One row: `slug`, `title`, `type`, `acceptance` (the bullets the reviewer grades one at a time),
   `verify` (slug of an extra verify node that will check you, usually null), `inputs`
   (`{name, shape, from, value}` — with `from`/`value` set it came from an upstream node; with both
   null it is external and its `shape` says where to find it), `outputs` (`{name, shape}` — you owe a
   value for each), `failed_criteria` (non-empty = this is a retry) and `notes` (`{topic, text, by}`).
   No row → reply `failed <slug>: no such node in the store` and stop.

3. **Use the notes before exploring.** Notes are hints from earlier agents. You alone apply the
   `setup` notes from your brief (the orchestrator never runs them): use them to provision your
   worktree and the `testing` notes to run your checks before you explore the repo to work out either;
   heed `conventions` and `gotcha`. A note never overrides this file, the acceptance, or the trust
   rules below.

4. **Check the registered helpers before writing a new one.**

   ```
   relate query --read-only --database <DB> --mode jsonl < <plugin>/cypher/symbols.cypher
   ```

   Each row (`name`, `file`, `purpose`, `by`) is a helper a completed node added. Reuse it rather than
   writing your own, then grep the repo for anything else that already does the job — the reviewer
   fails a diff that duplicates existing code or adds a third copy of the same logic.

5. **Do the work**, according to `type`:
   - **`code` / `test` / `chore`** — make the change **in `<worktree>`**, on the node branch, never in
     the main working tree: every edit, every check and every git command runs there

## REVIEW OBJECTIVE

Three checks, in order:

1. **Does every output field have a value matching its declared `shape`?** Run the mechanical check first:

   ```bash
   relate query --read-only --database <DB> --mode jsonl --param 'slug="<slug>"' --fetch-params result=<INBOX>/<slug>.json < <plugin>/cypher/check-result.cypher
   ```

   Any name in `missing_outputs` or `invalid_outputs` is a fail. Then judge each value against its
   `shape` yourself. A missing field, or a value that doesn't match its shape, is a fail regardless of the
   acceptance criteria — a downstream node reading it through `FROM` will break. Values must be scalars
   or lists of scalars; a nested value must be a JSON-encoded string.
2. **Does the output satisfy every bullet in `acceptance`, one at a time?** Not "does it seem fine
   overall" — go bullet by bullet, pass or fail each one individually, cite why. Most bullets settle
   from the diff plus the result file: when a bullet names something runnable and the diff shows it
   done, the implementer's green run stands — it already ran the check. Run a bullet's command
   yourself only when it is fast (seconds), when the diff leaves real doubt about it, or when
   `failed_criteria` names that bullet from an earlier attempt — and never the whole suite; that's
   the end-of-feature audit's job.
3. **Does the diff duplicate functionality, add a copy where an abstraction is due, or build beyond
   the bar?** For `research`/`decision`/`verify` nodes this is the YAGNI half only, judged on the
   outputs — they add no code. Otherwise, first list the helpers earlier nodes registered:

   ```bash
   relate query --read-only --database <DB> --mode jsonl < <plugin>/cypher/symbols.cypher
   ```

   Then size the sweep to the diff. Under ~30 changed lines
   (`git -C <worktree> diff --numstat <BRANCH>...HEAD`) skip the repo-wide grep: judge the diff
   closely against the registry — at that size a duplicate or a third copy is visible in the diff
   itself, and a reuse the registry missed is the end-of-feature audit's to catch. Otherwise grep
   the repo in `<worktree>`. The registry only holds symbols of completed, merged nodes —
   helpers from nodes running at the same time are unmerged and not in it (nor on this node's base), so
   never fault the diff for not reusing them. Search for an existing helper, utility, type, or pattern
   that already does what this node just built. If the node's core deliverable already exists, that's a
   fail — cite the code it should have reused. A partial overlap is an Issue citing the canonical code.
   Then count copies: if this diff adds a **third** copy of the same logic (the other two anywhere in the
   repo, elsewhere in the diff, or one of each), that's a missed abstraction and a fail — name all three
   sites and the shared helper that should own the logic. Two copies can stand; the third is where
   extracting beats copying. The counterweight is just as binding: YAGNI. Judge only copies that
   actually exist in the code today — never fault the diff for lacking an abstraction that only
   hypothetical future callers would use, and never treat a single concrete implementation left
   un-abstracted as a finding. YAGNI cuts the other way too, and there it is a fail: machinery no
   acceptance bullet or output needs — a speculative abstraction, an option or mode nothing reads, a
   refactor of code no criterion touches — is scope creep, not thoroughness. Fail it as
   `beyond the bar: <machinery> — <no criterion or output requires it>`, unless the repo's own
   established pattern asks for it; a minor extra is an `Issue` line, not a fail.

# Ship checklist

`plan` runs this checklist against the graph it just wrote, before handing off to `run`. Any item that
fails means revise the graph (with Cypher), not add a caveat in prose.

1. **Risky assumptions are resolved, not deferred.** Every assumption that would invalidate nodes or
   edges if wrong has either been confirmed against the codebase/docs, or is charted as a `research`
   node that answers it. An assumption left as "probably fine" is a hole.
2. **Every edge passes the cut test.** For each `DEPENDS_ON`, the dependent reads one of the
   dependency's `OUTPUT` fields through a `FROM` edge. `validate.cypher` rejects an edge with no data
   behind it and data with no edge behind it — but an agent can still invent a field just to satisfy it,
   so ask honestly whether the dependent *needs* that value.
3. **Independent nodes are actually in the same wave.** Read `wave` from `status.cypher` and confirm
   nodes with no real edge between them land together, not in a chain.
4. **Every node has non-empty, concrete, narrow acceptance criteria.** The schema requires a list and
   `validate.cypher` rejects blanks; `plan` itself is responsible for concrete — no `"looks correct"`, no
   criterion a fresh context couldn't check unaided — and for narrow: each criterion names the
   narrowest check that proves it, never a repo-wide suite where a scoped command would do. The
   implementer runs what criteria name and the reviewer re-runs it; the full suite belongs to the
   end-of-feature audit.
5. **Every `OUTPUT` field has a precise `shape`**, not free text. Downstream `INPUT` fields read it
   through `FROM` rather than re-describing it.
6. **Every `Acceptance` node is `SATISFIES`-covered** by at least one GbuildNode. An uncovered
   feature-level acceptance bullet means a node is missing. (`validate.cypher` enforces this.)
7. **No node restates a global acceptance bullet verbatim as its own criterion.** Node-level acceptance
   is the local, observable slice; the `Acceptance` nodes keep the whole-feature bar.
8. **Every controlled cycle has a hard round cap and a dedup rule**, stated in the node(s) that form the
   cycle — not left implicit.
9. **`DEPENDS_ON` is acyclic.** `validate.cypher` rejects a cycle; confirm it doesn't.
10. **Every `chore` node is depended on by at least one other node.** A chore nobody depends on isn't in
    scope — it's either wired wrong or shouldn't exist. (`validate.cypher` enforces this.)
11. **`failure_policy` fits the node type**, per `reference/failure-policies.md` — not defaulted to
    `retry` everywhere without thinking about it.
12. **`model_tier` is `strong` only where judgement, not throughput, is the bottleneck** — see
    `reference/cost-model.md`.
13. **No `research`, `decision` or `verify` node's acceptance requires a file change.** Those nodes edit
    no files (`graph-format.md`); an ADR, doc or other file a decision implies belongs to a `code` node
    reading the decision's outputs. `validate.cypher` can't see this — acceptance is free text — so check
    each one.
14. **The graph, run end to end with every node passing review, actually reaches `destination`.** Read
    the `Feature` node's `destination` property back against the node set: if every node completed, is
    the feature actually done? A graph that's internally consistent but doesn't add up to the
    destination is still wrong.
15. **`review` tier fits the node.** `mechanical` only where a named, scoped command or a shape check
    proves the whole bar (`reference/cost-model.md`); anything needing judgement to evaluate stays
    `reviewer`. A `mechanical` node whose acceptance isn't mechanically checkable has no gate at all.
16. **No node is smaller than its ceremony.** Every node costs a dispatch, a review, a worktree and a
    merge. Where two nodes' only relationship is one value passing between them, and a single context
    could hold both precisely, they are one node; where a cluster is all `cheap`, small and same-wave,
    note it for one-agent dispatch (`reference/cost-model.md`).

# Cost model

`plan` sets `model_tier` per node. `run` uses it to route model choice when the backend supports it
(the `Workflow` tool's `agent()` `model` option); the Agent-tool fallback treats it as a hint in the
dispatched agent's prompt when the harness offers a model choice, and otherwise ignores it — it is
never load-bearing for correctness, only cost.

## `cheap`

Default. Use for:

- `chore` nodes — mechanical, no judgement call.
- `test` nodes covering already-specified behavior.
- `code` nodes with a narrow, well-specified contract and concrete acceptance criteria (the review pass
  is what catches a cheap model's mistakes, not the model tier).
- `gbuild-reviewer` passes against short, mechanical acceptance lists.

## `strong`

Reserve for:

- `decision` nodes — the thing being bought is judgement, not throughput.
- `research` nodes where the answer requires synthesizing several sources, not just one lookup.
- `code` nodes whose contract is underspecified or whose acceptance criteria require judgement to
  evaluate (if a node needs `strong` for this reason, consider whether `plan` should have written
  tighter acceptance criteria instead).
- `verify` nodes doing adversarial or fact-checking work beyond the standard review.

## Review tiers

`plan` sets `review` per node (optional — unset means `reviewer`); `run` routes the gate on it.

- `reviewer` — the default. A fresh `gbuild-reviewer` grades the node: outputs against the contract,
  acceptance bullet by bullet, duplication, and the bar as a ceiling. Choose it whenever judging the
  output takes judgement — `code` nodes with any subtlety, `research`/`decision` nodes whose
  conclusions downstream nodes build on, anything whose acceptance a command can't fully prove.
- `mechanical` — no reviewer agent: `run` records the node on `check-result.cypher` alone (every
  output present and shape-valid), and the implementer's own green run of what the acceptance names
  is the correctness gate. A bad output surfaces when its consumer breaks, or in the end-of-feature
  audit. Choose it only where the acceptance is itself mechanical — a scoped command's exit status, a
  file's presence, a value's shape: most `chore` and `test` nodes, narrow lookups, and `code` nodes
  whose whole bar one scoped test run proves. If you can't name the command that proves the node, it
  isn't mechanical.

The tier is a trust decision `plan` owns, like `model_tier` and `failure_policy`: a graph that marks
everything `mechanical` has no gate but the audit; one that marks everything `reviewer` pays a
reviewer per node. Both errors are planning failures.

## Collapsing a cluster to one agent

When a wave's nodes are all `cheap`, tightly scoped, and small enough that one context could hold all
of them without losing precision, `plan` may note in the cluster's shape that `run` can dispatch them
as one agent handling the whole wave sequentially, rather than N concurrent agents — trading real
parallelism for lower overhead when the nodes are too small to be worth splitting. This is judgement
`plan` exercises at authoring time, not something `run` decides on its own; a wave `plan` didn't flag
this way is dispatched as one agent per node, per the default in `skills/run/SKILL.md`.

Never collapse nodes with different `failure_policy` values, or where any node in the cluster is
`strong` — those need to be dispatched (and possibly retried/repaired) independently.

# Talking to the gbuild store

Every gbuild skill reads and writes the feature store (modelled in `reference/graph-format.md`) with the
`relate` CLI and nothing else. `DB` throughout is the store path:
`<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/db` — beside the feature worktree, machine-local, never committed.
`INBOX` is `<git-common-dir>/gbuild/<feature>/inbox`, beside it: where `run`'s agents leave their result
files for `record.cypher` to read. This file is the full operating manual; the skills that only run
plugin scripts carry the short version of these rules inline.

## Requirement

`relate` 1.0.1 or newer must be on PATH. Check first, in every skill:

```
relate --version
```

If the command is missing or older than 1.0.1, stop and tell the user gbuild needs it:
`curl -sSfL https://relatedb.ai/install.sh | bash` (or `relate upgrade` for an existing
install). Never fall back to reading or editing `graph.json` by hand.

Two behaviors pin the floor. The ADR-0200 CLI cutover: the store path is a flag (`-d` /
`--database PATH`), the first positional is the Cypher statement (never the database), and piped
scripts and the interactive shell require the explicit `query` verb — the old path-first form,
database as the first argument, hard-fails. And ADR-0581: `--mode jsonl` prints pure rows
(§ Invocation), with the per-statement `planCache`/`timings` telemetry line behind `--timings`. On
an older binary a zero-row statement still ends with that telemetry line, so "no output = no rows"
stops being true — upgrade instead of parsing around it.

## One writer, one command at a time

The store is a directory store. A writable open takes its exclusive write lock; a `--read-only` open
does not, so read-only queries open the store beside a writer. Only a second writer fails, with
`storage locked` (exit 5). So:

- **Only the skill running in the main context writes to the store.** It is the only writer: schema,
  dispatch, record, set-status and authored writes run there and nowhere else.
- **Subagents may run read-only queries, never writes.** `run`'s implementers and reviewers read their
  own brief (`brief.cypher`), the helper registry (`symbols.cypher`) and their result check
  (`check-result.cypher`), always with `--read-only` — their agent files list exactly what they run.
  They report through files in `INBOX` plus a one-line reply; the orchestrator records them.
- **One `relate` command at a time from the main context** — no parallel tool calls on the store.
  Fan-out is for agents, not for store writes.
- On `storage locked` (exit 5), another writer holds the store (another gbuild command, a REPL left
  open). Wait a few seconds and retry, up to 3 times; then stop and report. Never delete
  `.cypherlite.lock`.

## Invocation

Always pass `--mode jsonl`: one compact JSON object per row, one row per line, and nothing else —
an N-row statement prints exactly N lines, a zero-row statement prints no line at all, so
**no output = no rows**. Never add `--timings`: it is the one flag that appends a
`{"planCache":…,"timings":{…}}` telemetry line per statement — a record that is not a row
(relate ≥ 1.0.1, ADR-0581). Every call is `relate query [STATEMENT] --database DB …`; with no STATEMENT the
piped stdin is the script list. Pure reads add `--read-only`: no exit flush, no lock (it opens beside
a writer, as above), and a fail-fast on a wrong path — a read-only call never creates a missing store.
Writes (schema creation, dispatch, record, set-status, authored heredocs) go without.

```
# a plugin read script
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/progress.cypher

# a plugin read script with parameters
relate query --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl --param 'slug="b-consume-doubled"' < ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/cypher/node.cypher

# an ad-hoc read — return only the columns you need, and keep a LIMIT on anything that can grow
relate query "MATCH (n:GbuildNode {status: 'failed'}) RETURN n.slug LIMIT 20" --read-only --database DB --mode jsonl

# a write you author (plan, reopen, fixes) — quoted heredoc delimiter, so the shell expands nothing
relate query --database DB <<'CYPHER'
.begin
MATCH (n:GbuildNode {slug: 'b-consume-doubled'}) SET n.title = 'Consume the value, double it';
.commit
CYPHER
```

## Rules

- **Read narrowly.** Prefer the smallest script that answers the question — `progress` for "how far
  along / is it done", `attention` for "what needs a decision", `dispatch` for "what runs next". The full
  per-node `status` is for the human-facing `/gbuild:status` report, not for loops.
- **Parameters are JSON.** Every `--param` value is JSON, single-quoted for the shell: strings in double
  quotes (`--param 'slug="01-scan-runners"'`), lists and objects as JSON (`--param 'slugs=["a","b"]'`).
  Bare values that start with a digit — timestamps, `01-…` slugs — are rejected, so always quote.
  `--fetch-params NAME=<file>` binds a JSON file as `$NAME` instead — how `record` and `check-result`
  read inbox files without anyone retyping them.
- **String literals** in Cypher you author: single quotes by default; double quotes when the text
  contains an apostrophe (`"gbuild's"`); backslash-escape (`\'`, `\"`) when it contains both.
- **Authored writes are atomic.** Wrap them in `.begin` / `.commit` — if any statement fails, the whole
  transaction is discarded. The plugin write scripts already do. Never write `.checkpoint`: a writable
  session checkpoints on exit by itself.
- **Values are scalars or lists of scalars.** Relate cannot store a map as a property value;
  JSON-encode anything nested into a string.
- **Read the result.** The plugin write scripts are guarded and return what they actually changed.
  Compare it with what you asked for; never assume a write landed.
- **Check the exit code.** `0` is success (an empty result included). `5` is `storage locked` or a
  write conflict — wait and retry as above. `6` is a rejected statement — syntax, semantic, or type
  error, including `ConstraintValidationFailed` and writes on a `--read-only` store — read stderr, fix,
  retry the whole transaction. `2` is a usage error — fix the invocation, not the data. `1` is any other
  runtime failure. With `--mode jsonl` a failure also prints one JSON error envelope on stdout, after
  any rows already written: `{"error":{"code","exit_code","kind","message","retryable"}}`.
- **Agent output is capped at 100 rows.** Under a detected agent harness with non-terminal stdout —
  gbuild skills always are — a statement prints at most 100 rows, warns on stderr, names the cut
  in-band with a `{"rowCap":…}` record (not a row either), and still exits `0`. Keep a `LIMIT` on
  anything that can grow; when you genuinely need every row, pass `--max-rows 0` (or
  set `RELATE_MAX_ROWS=0`).

Only `plan` does this, once per feature:

Stores charted by gbuild ≤ 0.7.1 live at `<tree>/.gbuild/<slug>/db` and are git-tracked. Migrate with
`git rm -r --cached .gbuild` (commit the removal) and
